false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

The export evaluates to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which yields the string value of the encryption key (not `true`) when both are set. Any consumer doing strict equality (`=== true`) or serializing/inspecting this flag will behave unexpectedly; export `!!(...)` instead.

Redirect URI change is unrelated and diverges from callback path derivation

The redirect URI was changed from the dynamic `` `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback` `` to the hardcoded `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback`. If appConfig.slug is ever renamed or the app is mounted under a different slug, add.ts and callback.ts (which still uses `${appConfig.slug}/callback` at line 36) will produce mismatched redirect URIs and Zoho will reject the token exchange. At minimum both files should derive the path the same way; ideally drop this unrelated drive-by change.

Sync request carries no authentication to the credential sync endpoint

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no auth header/signature, so any party that can reach the endpoint can request fresh OAuth tokens for arbitrary users. Since this endpoint hands out third-party access tokens, the request should be authenticated (e.g. with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) and ideally use HTTPS — neither is enforced or documented.

Sync-mode refresh response is fed to handleLarkError which expects Lark's envelope format

In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's response, but the code then runs `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, ...)` (line 84) which expects Lark's `{code: 0, data: {...}}` envelope, and builds new credentials from `data.data.refresh_token` / `data.data.refresh_expires_in`. Unless the self-hoster's endpoint happens to mimic Lark's exact envelope (undocumented), the refresh fails or produces undefined fields in the persisted key. The expected response contract for the sync endpoint is never defined and differs per app, making this integration unusable as written.

Token endpoint now hit on every Salesforce service instantiation

Previously jsforce refreshed tokens lazily via its own connection logic. The new getClient() unconditionally POSTs to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token and writes the credential row on every construction of SalesforceCalendarService (constructor awaits getClient). This means every booking operation involving Salesforce now performs an extra network round-trip and a DB write per request, even when the stored access token is still valid — a performance regression and unnecessary token churn for non-sync deployments.

Webhook secret compared with plain !== (non-constant-time) and header value may be an array

The secret check uses `!==` on `req.headers[...]`, which is a timing-observable comparison and, since Node header lookup can return string[] for repeated headers, a duplicate header could make the comparison fail unpredictably (or bypass intent if arrays are coerced). Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual) on a string-coerced header, as done for other webhook secrets in the codebase.

prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService

The new code added to getClient() calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (unlike every other service in this PR). Any use of the Salesforce calendar service will throw a ReferenceError/TS compile error as soon as the token refresh path runs, breaking Salesforce event creation and updates entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate and blacklist email checks are case-sensitive

Blacklist entries are lowercased (`email.toLowerCase()`) but then compared with `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` using the raw guest string, so `User@Example.com` bypasses a blacklisted `user@example.com`. Similarly `guest === attendee.email` is case-sensitive, so a guest already on the booking with different casing is re-added as a duplicate attendee row (and receives duplicate emails). Both the guest input and stored emails should be normalized (e.g. lowercased) before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of ||

The check `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))` requires the caller to be BOTH a team admin and a team owner. A team admin who is not an owner (the common case for delegated management) will fail this check even though the intent is clearly 'admin OR owner'. Use `||` so team admins can add guests to their team's bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email failure swallowed and wrong guests list passed to sendAddGuestsEmails

Two problems: (1) the catch block only logs `"Error sending AddGuestsEmails"` without the error object, so failures are undiagnosable and silently ignored; (2) `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is passed the raw input `guests` rather than the filtered `uniqueGuests`, so emails that were skipped (already attendees or blacklisted) are still treated as 'new' in email-manager's `newGuests.includes(...)` check (case-sensitively too), causing an existing attendee who was also submitted again to receive a full 'scheduled' email instead of the add-guests email.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Add-guests action offered for cancelled/past/unconfirmed bookings

The `add_members` entry is added unconditionally to `editBookingActions`, which is included in `bookedActions` for past and even cancelled bookings (cancel filter only removes the cancel action). Adding guests to a cancelled or already-ended booking still fires calendar updates and sends 'new guests added' confirmation emails for an event that no longer happens. The action should be gated on `!isCancelled` and the booking being in the future.

Any booking attendee can add arbitrary guests via the API

The handler authorizes any logged-in user whose email matches one of the booking's attendees (`isAttendee`). The UI only exposes this action to the organizer, but the tRPC mutation is callable by any authenticated attendee, letting an external guest with a cal.com account add unlimited arbitrary email addresses to someone else's booking (spam vector, data exposure of the event/ICS to arbitrary addresses). There is also no rate limit and no cap on the number of guests per request. Authorization should be restricted to the organizer / team admin.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` build the EventManager from the calling user. If the caller is an attendee or a team admin (not the booking organizer), the calendar update (`updateCalendarAttendees`) runs against the caller's calendar/credential set, not the booking owner's, so the guest update will be applied to the wrong calendar or fail. The organizer's credentials (already included in the booking query via `user.credentials`) should be used.

Error toast interpolates translation of a translation key that may not exist

`const message = \`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}\`` assumes `err.message` is a translation key present in common.json. TRPC errors thrown from other layers (e.g. Prisma or calendar update failures) return raw English messages or keys like `booking_not_found` that are not guaranteed to exist, producing a toast like `BAD_REQUEST: booking_not_found` untranslated. Also, the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never trigger since the template string is always non-empty.

No tests for the addGuests handler

The new mutation contains non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / team admin / attendee), dedup, blacklisting, and a calendar side effect, but the PR adds no integration or unit tests. The `&&` vs `||` admin bug (see separate finding) is exactly the kind of regression a permission test would have caught. At minimum, tests for the forbidden path, the duplicate-guest path, and the blacklist path should be added before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount incremented from stale in-memory value instead of atomic increment

The update writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read at query time. If two cron invocations overlap (or the handler is retried), both read the same retryCount and both write the same incremented value, so failures are undercounted and the retry limit is effectively never enforced. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete condition is not scoped to SMS reminders

The deleteMany OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the other branch. Any WorkflowReminder row of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount exceeds 1 will be deleted by this SMS cron job. Even though today only this file increments retryCount, the column is shared by all methods (WhatsApp reminders are handled by a separate cron, and the same retry pattern is likely to be reused there), so an email or WhatsApp reminder that failed twice would be silently destroyed by the SMS cron, dropping reminders that other schedulers still need. The retryCount condition should be ANDed with `method: SMS` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

false_positives.candidate:
Deletion of over-retried reminders happens a run late and deletes scheduled:false rows mid-cycle

Deletion of reminders with retryCount > 1 happens only at the start of the next cron run. A reminder that failed twice (retryCount = 2) is still picked up and scheduled again in the current run (the findMany does not filter retryCount), so it can actually be attempted 3 times, and the Twilio call happens before the deleteMany of the next run removes it. If the intent is 'delete after failing twice', the findMany should exclude retryCount >= 2, or the delete filter timing should be documented/adjusted. This also means a reminder that succeeds on the third attempt is then deleted by the next run's deleteMany (retryCount 2 > 1), discarding the referenceId needed to cancel the scheduled SMS.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests deleted while caching behavior still exists in the service

The previous test file contained a "Caching" describe block verifying that getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions return cached results on repeated calls. The service still implements this caching (cachedAuthConditions / cachedFilterConditions in insightsBooking.ts lines 84-95), but all coverage for it was removed rather than updated to the Prisma.Sql format. This is a regression in test coverage for behavior that remains in production code, including the subtle case where a cached `null` filter condition must not trigger a rebuild.

Final test queries BookingTimeStatusDenormalized but only inserts into Booking

The getBaseConditions test creates rows via `prisma.booking.create` and `prisma.eventType.create`, then runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ...` expecting the user booking's id to be returned. Unless BookingTimeStatusDenormalized is a live view or is populated by a trigger/denormalization job that runs synchronously on booking insert, the table will not contain the new row and the assertion will fail (or pass vacuously if rows are absent). The PR author notes the tests were never executed due to runner configuration issues, so this is unverified.

Passing JS arrays into Prisma.sql with = ANY(...) produces invalid SQL

In buildOrgAuthorizationCondition (line 164, `("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))`) and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition (line 201, `("userId" = ANY(${userIdsFromTeam}))`), a plain JavaScript array is interpolated directly into a Prisma.sql template. Prisma's sql tag does NOT bind a JS array as a single Postgres array parameter — it expands array elements into separate positional placeholders (which is why Prisma.join exists for IN lists). So `ANY(${[1,2,3]})` becomes `ANY($1, $2, $3)`, which is a Postgres syntax/runtime error, or worse, `ANY($1)` with a scalar when the array has one element, silently matching nothing. The correct construction is `ANY(${Prisma.sql`ARRAY[${Prisma.join(teamIds)}]::int[]`})` or equivalent. The tests at lines 296 and 333 of the integration test compare against Prisma.sql templates built the same wrong way, so a deep-equal structural comparison can pass even though the generated query is broken when actually executed — and the PR description explicitly states the tests were never run.

findMany() removed, breaking existing callers of the service

The diff deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method, which accepted Prisma BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs and returned typed rows. It is replaced only by `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, which returns a raw SQL fragment that callers must embed into a hand-written raw query themselves. Any existing caller (e.g. insights repositories/routes that did `service.findMany({ select, orderBy, where })`) will fail to compile or, if untyped, fail at runtime. There is no deprecation shim or migration in this PR; the maintainer must verify every call site has been converted to $queryRaw with correct table names, select lists, and ordering before merging.

toEqual on Prisma.Sql objects may not validate actual SQL correctness

All condition tests compare results with `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql\`...\`)`. Prisma.Sql equality via vitest's deep equality only compares the internal strings/values structure; it does not verify the fragment is executable SQL. Combined with the fact that the author states the tests were never run, the expectations could match structurally while the produced SQL is invalid when executed (see the ANY(array) finding). At least one test per code path should execute the condition against the database via $queryRaw, as only the final test attempts to do.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data object will throw at runtime

The new call `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object. Prisma's `updateMany` rejects an empty `data` argument with a validation error ("Argument `data` must provide at least one field"). Since the comment says the intent is to bump `updatedAt`, this call will throw every time `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` completes (i.e. on every calendar watch/unwatch cycle), breaking webhook-driven cache refresh. It should pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only and fails on Linux

`sed -i '' -E ...` uses the BSD/macOS form of in-place editing; on GNU/Linux (Linux CI/dev containers) `sed -i ''` fails with "can't read : No such file or directory". Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak` + remove the backup) or detect the platform.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache status timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale, ignoring user locale

The component formats `cacheUpdatedAt` with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the user's selected locale even though the component already has `useLocale()`. All non-English users will see US-formatted dates. Should use the locale from `useLocale()`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status lookup misses caches stored for in-memory delegation credentials

For in-memory delegation credentials (negative credentialId), `CalendarCache` rows are keyed by `userId` + key rather than the (nonexistent) DB credentialId (see `CalendarCacheRepository.getCachedAvailability`). `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` only groups by `credentialId`, so delegated Google Calendar users will never see their cache status and cannot clear it from the UI, even though a cache exists and is actively served. Either look up by userId for delegation credentials or document the limitation.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status

On successful cache deletion, the component only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback (which is only passed as `onChanged` in some usages). It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, unlike the disconnect mutation. If `onChanged` is undefined or does not refetch, the UI continues to show the old "Cache Status / Last updated" entry and the "Delete cached data" option even though the cache is gone, until a manual page refresh.

dev:cron uses npx tsx but tsx is not a declared dependency

The script was changed from `ts-node` to `npx tsx`, but `tsx` is not in dependencies or devDependencies (only `ts-node` is, and it remains unused for this script). `npx` will download `tsx` ad hoc on each run (or fail offline / behind a proxy). Add `tsx` to devDependencies.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds reports expired cache entries as active

The groupBy query does not filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. A credential whose only cache rows have expired will still return an `updatedAt` value, so the UI will show a "Cache Status / Last updated" timestamp and a "Delete cached data" action for cache data that is no longer served. This is misleading and lets users trigger a no-op delete with a confirmation dialog.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget and not awaited

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async functions but are called inside `forEach` without awaiting (same pattern in packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:966, packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx:488 and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx in the delete/update handlers). The handler responds and continues (e.g. deletes attendees and booking references) while the cancellation DB update / SendGrid / Twilio calls are still in flight. Besides unhandled rejections, in workflows.tsx `delete` the subsequent `workflow.deleteMany` cascades to workflowStep and deletes the workflowReminder rows, which can race with the pending `prisma.workflowReminder.update({cancelled: true})` and make it fail with P2025 (silently caught), leaving the scheduled email uncancellable. All cancellation calls should be collected and awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path never marks or deletes the DB row, so a failed SendGrid cancel is unrecoverable

In `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, when `immediateDelete` is true the function only issues the SendGrid cancel request and returns; it never sets `cancelled: true` and never deletes the workflowReminder row. If the SendGrid request fails (network error, invalid batch id, rate limit), the error is swallowed by the catch and the row remains `scheduled: true, cancelled: null`. The cron job only cancels reminders with `cancelled: true`, so there is no retry: the email is still sent even though the booking was rescheduled (handleNewBooking uses `immediateDelete=true` for reschedules). The failure should set `cancelled: true` as a fallback so the cron can retry, or the row should be deleted/marked after a confirmed cancel.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New `cancelled` column is nullable with no default, weakening queries and invariants

The migration adds `cancelled BOOLEAN` (nullable, no default) to WorkflowReminder. Existing and new rows have `cancelled = null` rather than `false`, so filters like `cancelled: true` work but any future filter for 'not cancelled' must treat null, and the Prisma type is `boolean | null` everywhere. `Boolean @default(false)` would make the semantics explicit and the cron queries simpler/safer.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation loop aborts entirely on the first SendGrid failure

The per-reminder SendGrid cancel request is inside a single try/catch wrapping the whole loop. One failing request (e.g. a stale/invalid batch_id for a reminder whose email was already sent) throws, skips the DB delete for that reminder and skips cancelling every subsequent reminder in `remindersToCancel` for this run; the failed reminder will fail again on every future run, permanently blocking the rest of the queue. Each reminder should be cancelled and deleted inside its own try/catch.

Cancellation only happens within 1 hour of the scheduled date, allowing late cron runs to miss emails

Reminders are only cancelled once `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, and the cron runs every 15 minutes. A booking cancelled shortly before a reminder's scheduled date (e.g. 10 minutes before) will only be processed at the next cron tick, which can be after the email has already been sent by SendGrid. There is no compensation for this window (e.g. cancelling immediately when the request comes in, or SendGrid-side suppression), so the original bug ('cancelled bookings still receive reminders') persists for reminders close to their send time.

Cancellation query does not filter by method EMAIL, so SendGrid is called with Twilio SIDs

The `remindersToCancel` query only filters on `cancelled: true` and scheduledDate, without `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. If a non-email (SMS) reminder row ever ends up with `cancelled: true`, the loop will POST its Twilio message SID to the SendGrid `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` endpoint as a `batch_id`. That request fails, the thrown error is caught by the surrounding try/catch which aborts the whole loop, and all remaining email reminders in the batch are left uncancelled (and their DB rows undeleted) for that run. Each reminder should be cancelled/deleted individually with per-reminder error handling, and the query should filter `method: EMAIL`.

If Twilio cancelSMS fails the reminder row is not deleted and never retried

In `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, if `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` throws, the subsequent `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` is skipped (the catch swallows the error). The row survives with its referenceId, but nothing ever retries the cancellation — the callers have already moved on — so the SMS is still sent for a cancelled/rescheduled booking. The Twilio cancel and the DB delete should be decoupled so a Twilio failure doesn't prevent cleanup, or the row should be marked for retry like the email path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach callback results discarded; deletion errors become unhandled rejections

Same issue as vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` fire-and-forgets the async work. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so sync errors were caught by the enclosing try/catch; after this change, rejections from the dynamic import or getCalendar escape the try/catch as unhandled promise rejections, and the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and return `true` regardless of whether calendar/video events were actually deleted. Await the collected promises instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-booking calendar deletions are fire-and-forget and may never run before the request completes

In the allRemainingBookings branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` uses an async callback inside forEach. Nothing awaits these promises: `apiDeletes` is later consumed via `await apiDeletes;` (line 617), which awaits a plain array (a no-op), and `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 can run before the async forEach bodies have pushed anything (the first `await getCalendar(credential)` yields before any deleteEvent is pushed). Consequence: when cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, external calendar events may not be deleted at all, or deleted after the response/DB cleanup, and any failures surface as unhandled promise rejections. Replace with `for...of`/`Promise.all` and actually await the resulting promises.

false_positives.candidate:
All dynamic imports are started eagerly at module evaluation; failed chunk loads produce unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")` (and all others) at module-evaluation time, so merely importing `@calcom/app-store` kicks off loading every app chunk immediately — the lazy-loading benefit only applies to bundling, not to runtime loading, and on the server every app module is still loaded whenever app-store is imported. Additionally, if any of these top-level import promises rejects (e.g. a broken app build), it becomes an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the Node process even for code paths that never use that app. Wrap the entries in functions/thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) or attach a rejection handler so failures are surfaced only to the code that awaits them.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not a promise — deletion failures are silently ignored on paid-booking cancellation

In the paid-booking branch, `await apiDeletes;` awaits a plain Array (which resolves immediately), so none of the calendar/video deletion promises pushed into apiDeletes are actually awaited before returning "Booking successfully cancelled.". Combined with this PR's change to push into apiDeletes from an async forEach callback (line 460-470), deletions may not even have been started yet. Use `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)` so integration deletions complete (and failures are observed) before responding.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares UTC slot hours to organizer-local working hours and computes wrong end

The new working-hours validation computes `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — start and end are identical, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends past workingHour.endTime is never rejected (end should be start + eventLength). Additionally, `slotStartTime` is a UTC dayjs (time.utc()), so `hour()` returns the UTC hour, while `workingHour.startTime/endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's timezone. For any organizer not on UTC the comparison is off by the organizer's UTC offset, so valid slots get rejected and invalid ones accepted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object-identity comparison of dayjs instances is always false

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two distinct dayjs object references with `===`, which is always false regardless of values. The intended zero-length-override (unavailability) check is dead code and never fires; presumably `.isSame(...)` was meant.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix described in the PR

The PR's headline fix (date overrides of fixed hosts constraining round-robin availability) has no corresponding test: the only new test re-checks the personal-event timezone behavior, and the existing ROUND_ROBIN tests use plain IstWorkHours schedules without date overrides for the fixed host. A regression in the checkIfIsAvailable changes (e.g., the busy-time bypass or the broken working-hours comparison) would not be caught for the round-robin scenario the PR claims to fix.

Override times that cross midnight after offset conversion produce inverted minute ranges

The override startTime/endTime are computed as `hour() * 60 + minute()` after applying the invitee-organizer offset. If the shift moves the override start or end across midnight (e.g., an organizer override ending at 00:30 local), the minute-of-day arithmetic produces a wrong or inverted range (endTime < startTime), which buildSlots then discards (`if (start >= end) continue`) or clips incorrectly, silently dropping availability that should exist. There is no handling for day rollover introduced by the offset.

Selected-slots filter drops dateOverrides and workingHours, weakening availability check

In the final selectedSlots filter (line ~581), checkIfIsAvailable is called with `busy`, `...availabilityCheckProps`, and `organizerTimeZone`, but without the host's `dateOverrides` or `workingHours`. For events with seat selection or reserved slots, the date-override logic just added elsewhere is not applied here, so behavior differs between the fixed/loose host checks and this path; slots that should be blocked by a fixed host's date override can still be returned in this branch.

Slots inside a date override bypass all busy-time checks

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot falls on a day that has a date override and the slot is inside the override window, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true and the function returns true immediately (lines 133-135), never reaching the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom. Consequence: a fixed host (or any host) who has a calendar event or an accepted Cal booking during the override window will still be reported as available for that slot, allowing double bookings — the exact class of bug this PR claims to fix for round-robin. The override check should mark the slot as within-override and then still evaluate busy times.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
No test that multiple flusher processes actually flush their shards end-to-end

The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts process/shard bookkeeping (counts and map sizes); it never submits a span or asserts that a segment is produced. There is no test covering the core new behavior: that with multiple flusher processes, spans on shards assigned to different processes are all flushed exactly once, nor a test for the restart path (`_ensure_processes_alive` with multiple processes), which is where the trickiest new logic lives. A regression in shard-to-process mapping or in restart handling would pass the current test suite.

Restart counter never resets, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer even if each process is healthy

`process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented; there is no reset after a process proves itself healthy. With MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10, a shard-group that legitimately restarts 11 times over the entire lifetime of a long-running consumer (e.g. due to transient Redis/Kafka failures hours apart) will trigger `RuntimeError` and crash the whole consumer, taking down all shard flushers. The counter should reset (or decay) after a period of healthy operation, as was the case before this change for the single process — but this PR now makes it much more likely since a single misbehaving shard-group among many takes the consumer down.

Restarting a 'hung' process can run two flushers on the same shards, producing duplicate segments

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), `process.kill()` is called and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards`. `kill()` is asynchronous — the old process can still be inside its flush loop while the new process starts flushing the same shards. Both processes can call `buffer.flush_segments()` and produce the same segments to Kafka before either calls `done_flush_segments`, resulting in duplicate segments in the buffered-segments topic (duplicate span data downstream). The old process is also never joined, so it is never confirmed dead before the replacement starts. The replacement should only be started after the old process has actually exited (join with timeout), and ideally after verifying no in-flight flush.

Thread-based flusher (produce_to_pipe path) is never killed on restart, so restarts stack threads

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, the flusher 'process' is a `threading.Thread`. On an unhealthy restart, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so the old thread is left running and a new one is spawned for the same shards. A hung thread never recovers, so every restart adds another thread; if the hang is caused by a stuck `produce` (as in the backpressure test, where append sleeps), multiple threads will flush the same shards concurrently, duplicating messages. This mostly affects the test path today, but the code claims Thread support, so it should either kill/stop the old thread cooperatively (e.g. per-process stop flag) or refuse to restart thread-based flushers.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` with a process index directly). It also has a bug if it were used: it would overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous process. It should be removed.

submit() iterates self.buffers while restarts mutate it

`submit()` and `_ensure_processes_alive()` run on the main thread, so the dict mutation itself is not racy in-process. However `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.buffers[process_index]` with a brand new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each restart. If a restart happens between the `record_stored_segments()` loop and the memory-info loop within a single `submit()` call, some shards' buffers get recorded twice and some not at all within that call; more importantly each restart allocates a new SpansBuffer (with new Redis clients) while old ones are never closed, leaking Redis connections over repeated restarts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
--max-workers help text/semantics conflate worker threads and queue count

In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. Consider documenting the remapping caveat and the differing default.

Background commit thread commits without regard to partition ownership

The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, giving at-most-once semantics

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and only logged (line 144-147), and the finally block at line 149 always calls offset_tracker.complete_offset. The offset is then treated as processed and will be committed by the commit loop. Combined with ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 53-54) which also swallows all exceptions, any transient failure (e.g. a DB error while handling a result) silently drops the message and advances the committed offset past it, so the message is never retried. This contradicts the class docstring's guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns the consumer into an at-most-once pipeline with silent data loss.

Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, breaking rebalance recovery

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. The queue_pool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key uses the raw subject identifier, not the resolved user UID

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID (the raw ID parsed from the subject string), whereas the permission cache key (userPermCacheKey) is built from the resolved userIdentifiers.UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:360, 379). Since GetUserIdentifiers accepts both numeric user IDs and UIDs as the subject identifier (service.go:463-469), the same user can be addressed as 'user:112' or 'user:<uid>'. The denial decision was computed from the resolved identity's permissions, but it is stored under the caller-supplied identifier. Consequences: (1) denial entries are not shared between the two spellings, causing unnecessary duplicate DB requeries; (2) if the mapping between a numeric ID and UID ever changes (user deletion/recreation), a stale denial entry keyed by the numeric ID remains valid and keeps denying the new identity for up to 30s. The key should use the resolved UID, consistent with the permission cache.

Denial cache reintroduces the 'cannot access newly created resource' bug the PR fixes

The permDenialCache entry for (namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder) is set with a 30s TTL whenever a Check is denied, and any later Check with the same key short-circuits to denied before the permission cache or DB is consulted (service.go:116-121). Consider the exact scenario the PR describes: a user without a scoped permission triggers a Check for e.g. dashboards:read on name 'newdash' in folder 'fold1' (e.g. a pre-flight check, a duplicate-name check, or a failed attempt), which populates a denial entry. The user then creates the dashboard/folder, which writes the permission row to the DB. The next Check for that same (user, action, name, folder) hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false without ever re-querying the DB — so the creator is still locked out of their newly created resource for up to 30 seconds. Any mechanism that invalidates/refreshes permCache (e.g. a DB requery triggered by a different resource name) does not invalidate the denial entry, so the denial can even outlive a freshly queried permission map that would allow the request. The denial cache needs to be invalidated when permissions change (e.g. on permission/role writes or resource creation), or its scope/TTL must be bounded so it cannot mask fresh grants.

Denial-cache hits are counted as permission-cache hits in metrics

When the denial cache short-circuits a Check, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit). This conflates the new denial cache with the permission cache, making the permissionCacheUsage metric misleading for operators tuning cache behavior: a denial hit is reported as a permission cache hit even though the permission cache was never consulted. A separate label or metric (e.g. permissionDenialCacheUsage) should be used.

No test covers the denial cache being populated by a denied Check and its interaction with later allowed checks

The only denial-cache test ('Should deny on explicit cache deny entry') manually pre-populates permDenialCache; there is no test that a Check returning Allowed=false actually writes a denial entry and that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits without touching the store. More importantly, there is no test for the interaction the feature exists for: after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant of the permission in the store (simulating resource creation) — the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sibling case where permCache/DB allow but the denial entry denies. Without such a test the stale-denial regression risk (denial entry masking a fresh DB allow) is unguarded.
