true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the all-clients resource does not exist in hasPermission(ClientModel, String)

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no per-client resource exists, the code calls AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately passes the result to authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource). getResourceTypeResource explicitly returns null when the resource type is unknown or no resource with that name exists (which is exactly the situation for realms initialized before this change, or if the "Clients" resource was never created). findByResource(server, null) will then throw a NullPointerException (or store-dependent error), turning a permission check into a 500 instead of returning false. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: in `hasPermission`, `getResourceTypeResource` can return null, which is then passed to `findByResource` causing a `NullPointerException`, and requires a null check.

false_positives.candidate:
Client deletion throws UnsupportedOperationException with V2 enabled via the ClientRemovedEvent listener

AdminPermissions.registerListener() handles ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent by calling management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). Before this PR, MgmtPermissionsV2 did not override clients(), so the V1 ClientPermissions implementation was used and this call worked. Now clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled() throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The listener guard only checks Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1), which is typically enabled together with V2, so deleting any client in a realm where the fine-grained admin authz features are active will throw an exception inside the provider-event listener, likely failing or corrupting the client-removal flow. setPermissionsEnabled (and the other inherited V1 methods that no longer have a working implementation) need a no-op/compat implementation, or the listener must skip the clients branch for V2.

No migration for realms that already initialized the admin permissions client: new Clients resource and scopes are never created

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null. Any realm that enabled admin permissions before this change has a resource server containing only the Users resource type and only the Users scopes (manage, view, impersonate, map-roles, manage-group-membership). The new scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) and the "Clients" all-resource will never be created for such realms. Consequences: creating a Clients scope permission will fail (getScope lookup fails or resource lookup in getOrCreateResource finds nothing and throws "Could not map resource object..."), and ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission can hit a null "Clients" resource (see separate NPE finding). A migration step (or extending init() to create missing scopes/resources for existing admin permission clients) is required.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking token-exchange permission evaluation paths

canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. This method is part of the ClientPermissions contract used by token-exchange admin/permission evaluation code that is not gated on the V2 feature flag; if any of those paths execute while V2 is enabled, the caller receives a 500 error instead of an authorization decision. Either the V2 implementation must provide a decision (e.g., delegate to the scope-based evaluation or deny), or all call sites must be verified to be unreachable under V2 — with the unreachable ones documented/tested. The same concern applies to the other thrown methods if any remaining code path (e.g., the registerListener cleanup path) invokes them.

Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. false_positives.candidate:
NPE when per-group resource and all-groups resource are both absent

In hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes), when `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` returns null, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`, which returns null whenever the resource type resource does not exist or the schema is not supported for the resource server. getSubGroups previously computed `canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()` once and short-circuited the filter. Now `auth.groups()::canView` is evaluated per subgroup. For an admin without the manage-users/view-users roles, each invocation of the V1 (and V2) global canView() runs a full authorization-policy evaluation against the admin permissions resource server, so listing a group with many subgroups performs N policy evaluations instead of one. Either this asymmetry is intentional (then it deserves a comment) or the group path/name lookup is missing; as written, the API behaves inconsistently across resource types and callers passing a group path get a 500-level error.

In getScope, when the schema is supported, `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType)` is dereferenced without a null check. A null/unknown-type check with a meaningful validation error is needed.

DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider previously threw an IllegalStateException when multiple providers were found; now it silently picks the first after sorting, but the sort is stable only relative to ServiceLoader iteration order, which depends on classpath ordering. In a deployment that (accidentally or intentionally) has more than one of these providers on the classpath, e.g. a FIPS environment where keycloak-crypto-fips1402 and keycloak-crypto-default are both present, the non-FIPS provider may win arbitrarily, silently disabling FIPS mode. Either the FIPS provider should have a strictly higher order, or ties among full-featured providers should still be reported as an error.

Most CryptoProvider operations throw UnsupportedOperationException, breaking authz-client features beyond ECDSA signature conversion

The provider registered via META-INF/services in the authz-client jar throws UnsupportedOperationException for getPemUtils(), getCertificateUtils(), getX509CertFactory(), getKeyFactory(), getSignature(), getAlgorithmProvider() etc. CryptoIntegration.init is now called from AuthzClient.create, so if this is the only provider discoverable via the AuthzClient classloader, any code path in keycloak-common/authz-client that touches those APIs will fail at runtime — for example parsing PEM keys/certificates for client JWT assertion signing, or JWKS handling. Previously, these paths worked whenever BC was on the classpath via DefaultCryptoProvider; now a working deployment can regress to UnsupportedOperationException. Each unsupported method should either be implemented with JCE defaults (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or the design should ensure DefaultCryptoProvider is used when available.

Test uses one default-curve key pair for all algorithms and only checks round-trip, not interop with the BC implementation

The test generates a single key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") without specifying a curve, so ES384/ES512 cases run with (typically) a P-256 key and only exercise zero-padding logic, never real 48/66-byte coordinates. More importantly, it only verifies that this provider's conversion round-trips with itself; it does not compare output against DefaultCryptoProvider/BouncyCastle (e.g., BCECDSACryptoProvider) to guarantee signature compatibility with what the Keycloak server produces/expects. A cross-check against the BC implementation per curve would catch subtle encoding mismatches (leading-zero handling, negative integers) that a self-round-trip cannot.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarting a 'hung' process can run two flushers on the same shards, producing duplicate segments

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), `process.kill()` is called and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards`. `kill()` is asynchronous — the old process can still be inside its flush loop while the new process starts flushing the same shards. Both processes can call `buffer.flush_segments()` and produce the same segments to Kafka before either calls `done_flush_segments`, resulting in duplicate segments in the buffered-segments topic (duplicate span data downstream). The old process is also never joined, so it is never confirmed dead before the replacement starts. The replacement should only be started after the old process has actually exited (join with timeout), and ideally after verifying no in-flight flush.

Thread-based flusher (produce_to_pipe path) is never killed on restart, so restarts stack threads

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, the flusher 'process' is a `threading.Thread`. On an unhealthy restart, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so the old thread is left running and a new one is spawned for the same shards. A hung thread never recovers, so every restart adds another thread; if the hang is caused by a stuck `produce` (as in the backpressure test, where append sleeps), multiple threads will flush the same shards concurrently, duplicating messages. This mostly affects the test path today, but the code claims Thread support, so it should either kill/stop the old thread cooperatively (e.g. per-process stop flag) or refuse to restart thread-based flushers.

Restart counter never resets, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer even if each process is healthy

`process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented; there is no reset after a process proves itself healthy. With MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10, a shard-group that legitimately restarts 11 times over the entire lifetime of a long-running consumer (e.g. due to transient Redis/Kafka failures hours apart) will trigger `RuntimeError` and crash the whole consumer, taking down all shard flushers. The counter should reset (or decay) after a period of healthy operation, as was the case before this change for the single process — but this PR now makes it much more likely since a single misbehaving shard-group among many takes the consumer down.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` with a process index directly). It also has a bug if it were used: it would overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous process. It should be removed.

No test that multiple flusher processes actually flush their shards end-to-end

The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts process/shard bookkeeping (counts and map sizes); it never submits a span or asserts that a segment is produced. There is no test covering the core new behavior: that with multiple flusher processes, spans on shards assigned to different processes are all flushed exactly once, nor a test for the restart path (`_ensure_processes_alive` with multiple processes), which is where the trickiest new logic lives. A regression in shard-to-process mapping or in restart handling would pass the current test suite.

submit() iterates self.buffers while restarts mutate it

`submit()` and `_ensure_processes_alive()` run on the main thread, so the dict mutation itself is not racy in-process. However `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.buffers[process_index]` with a brand new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each restart. If a restart happens between the `record_stored_segments()` loop and the memory-info loop within a single `submit()` call, some shards' buffers get recorded twice and some not at all within that call; more importantly each restart allocates a new SpansBuffer (with new Redis clients) while old ones are never closed, leaking Redis connections over repeated restarts.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds and lost index writes

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its whole duration, which (despite the perf cost) guaranteed only one index per NamespacedResource was ever built and published to the cache. Now the lock is only taken around `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two callers can build the same key concurrently: during `searchSupport.init` (multi-worker errgroup) and via `getOrCreateIndex` triggered by a watch event or a Search request arriving while init is still building. Consequences: (1) two bleveIndex objects exist for the same key; the loser of the last cache write keeps getting writes (e.g. from handleEvent) into an index that is no longer in the cache, so those documents silently vanish from search results — data loss for the index; (2) for file-backed indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both builds call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, which will fail (index already exists) or corrupt the on-disk index. getOrCreateIndex's own TODO comment ("we don't want to block while anything is building, just the same key") confirms per-key serialization is required; this change removed even the coarse serialization without adding a per-key one.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in BuildIndex caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock to only cover the final cache assignment, allowing concurrent duplicate builds for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now performs full index build synchronously, changing the constructor contract for all callers

Init() (which builds the entire search index over all namespaces and can take a long time on large installations) is now invoked inside NewResourceServer, and any init failure makes the constructor return an error. Previously, callers such as embedded/in-process usage of the resource server (e.g. apiserver storage wiring, tests, single-binary Grafana where the unified storage may be created alongside other services) got a server immediately and initialization happened lazily or in the background. Those callers now block startup for the whole index build and will fail hard if the index build errors (e.g. transient DB issue during startup), where previously reads/writes could still be served. The PR description itself flags this ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") — the callers of NewResourceServer outside the storage-server target need to be audited; no such audit or feature flag is included.

Failed Init in constructor leaks the server's background context and goroutines

When s.Init(ctx) fails inside NewResourceServer, the function returns nil, err, but s.cancel() is never called. Init may have already started background work before failing — notably searchSupport.init's watch-event goroutine (started after WatchWriteEvents succeeds) and the lifecycle hooks' partial initialization. With no reference to the server retained by the caller, those goroutines and the cancelable context are leaked for the life of the process. The error path should call s.cancel() (or s.Stop) before returning.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in init's worker goroutines

In searchSupport.init, the loop over stats spawns goroutines (limited by initWorkers, so several run concurrently) that both execute `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assign `_, _, err = s.build(...)` where `err` is the outer function-scope variable declared at `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`. These are unsynchronized concurrent read/writes of shared variables — a data race under Go's memory model (and `go test -race` will flag it), and the shared `err` can be clobbered by a later goroutine, causing a real build error to be lost so init reports success with a missing index. Each goroutine should use its own local counter/err (e.g. `i, e := 0, error(nil)` captured per closure), with totals aggregated after group.Wait().

Watch event goroutine has no termination path and panics on closed channel

The goroutine started at the end of init reads `v := <-events` in an infinite loop with no select on a done channel. When the storage backend closes the events channel (e.g. the SQL poller exits when b.done fires on Stop, which closes the stream), the receive yields nil forever and s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) dereferences evt.Type/evt.Key, panicking the process. Additionally, because this uses context.Background(), there is no way to stop it on shutdown. Now that init runs in the constructor for the storage-server target, every server start creates this goroutine, so it must be tied to the server's cancelable context.

Init ordering change: watch events consumed by searchSupport.init but broadcaster started after — event gap risk and misordering rationale

The diff moves initWatcher() to after s.search.init(). searchSupport.init internally starts its own WatchWriteEvents subscription, so this ordering is intentional (watch events are captured while the index builds). However, the server's broadcaster (used by the Watch RPC) is only started after the potentially long index build completes. During that window, Watch RPCs that do reach the server (the gRPC server may already be serving since the module server registers services before/around construction) will fail or block on s.broadcaster — notably s.broadcaster is nil until initWatcher succeeds, so a Watch call during init will nil-pointer panic on `s.broadcaster.Subscribe`. At minimum the nil broadcaster needs a guard, or initWatcher should run before search init (with search's own event subscription providing continuity, which is the pre-existing design).

Storage-server integration test disabled for postgres with no follow-up issue

The only integration test covering the storage-server target (which is exactly the code path changed by this PR — eager init of unified storage at startup) is now skipped for postgres with a TODO comment ("not working with postgres in Drone"). This means the main behavioral change in this PR (synchronous index init at startup) has no integration coverage on one of the two supported databases, and the failure cause is neither diagnosed nor tracked. Since this test is the regression guard for the change, the skip should be replaced by a fix or linked to a tracked issue.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. The queue_pool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. A separate label or metric (e.g. permissionDenialCacheUsage) should be used.

The only denial-cache test ('Should deny on explicit cache deny entry') manually pre-populates permDenialCache; there is no test that a Check returning Allowed=false actually writes a denial entry and that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits without touching the store. More importantly, there is no test for the interaction the feature exists for: after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant of the permission in the store (simulating resource creation) — the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sibling case where permCache/DB allow but the denial entry denies. Without such a test the stale-denial regression risk (denial entry masking a fresh DB allow) is unguarded.

If an admin picks an alias level (e.g. 'everyone') in the new-group form, the group is created with alias_level 0 and the selection is silently lost. The update action (line 37) does honor params[:alias_level], so the two actions are inconsistent.

Remove-member link rendered for automatic groups

The template gates the remove link on {{#unless automatic}}, but this partial is rendered by the group-member item view whose context is the individual member (a Discourse.User), not the group. The member user object has no 'automatic' property, so the guard is always truthy-negative and the remove link is shown for automatic groups too (where the parent group.hbs template deliberately hides the add-members UI for automatic groups). Clicking it triggers removeMember on an automatic group, which the server rejects with a 422 and no user-visible error handling. The view should receive the group's automatic flag explicitly (e.g. via a computed property on the view or controller).

add_members returns success even when no users matched

add_members splits the username list and skips any username that doesn't match a user (the `if user = User.find_by_username(username)` guard), then unconditionally renders success_json. An admin who typos a username in the add-members box gets a success response and a member list refresh that doesn't contain the user, with no indication anything failed. The action should report which usernames could not be added (render_json_error) so the UI can surface it.

Public members endpoint allows unbounded limit

The members action takes `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` with no upper bound, on a route reachable by any logged-in (and possibly anonymous, subject to visibility) user. Passing limit=1000000 makes the server serialize up to a million member records in one response. The previous code capped the practical default at 200 for automatic groups; the new code should clamp limit to a sane maximum (e.g. 1000) before using it in the query.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs writes (match_count increment) inside model validation

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block? during User validation, and should_block? increments match_count and saves the record. In UsersController#create the user is validated via user.valid? (line 168) and then validated again by user.save, so each blocked signup attempt increments match_count twice and issues two UPDATE statements. Validations should be side-effect free; the statistics update should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed save) to avoid inflated counts, unnecessary writes, and unexpected behavior when a model is validated for other reasons.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying architectural flaw: the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (or `should_block_email?`) predicate method performs database writes (updating statistics/incrementing `match_count`) as a side effect of a read/validation check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: BlockedEmail.where(email: email). An attacker (or ordinary user) whose address is on the block list can register as "Bad@SpamClub.com" when the list contains "bad@spamclub.com" and the check will not match. The lookup should compare normalized (downcased/stripped) emails, e.g. where(email: Email.downcase(email)).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is case-sensitive, allowing blocked users to bypass the check by changing the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is not atomic

should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. Under concurrent requests two processes can read the same count and both write count+1, losing increments. Use BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now]) or an atomic counter update.

change_email endpoint is not covered by the blocked-email check

The new EmailValidator (with the BlockedEmail check) only runs when email_changed? on a User record, but UsersController#change_email never assigns the new email to the user — it directly creates an email_token with the new address and sends the confirmation mail. A user can therefore sign up with an unblocked address and then switch to a blocked address via change_email, completely bypassing the blocked-email feature. The controller should also call BlockedEmail.should_block?(lower_email) (and the whitelist/blacklist check) before creating the token.

Blocked check silently skipped when a domain-restriction error was already added

The blocked-email check only runs if record.errors[attribute].blank?. If the email fails the whitelist/blacklist check, should_block? is never called, so match_count/last_match_at statistics for that blocked email are not recorded. This makes the analytics fields unreliable and the ordering dependency between the two checks is fragile (a future error added earlier would silently disable the block check). The block check should run independently of prior errors.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid -ms-align-items property in align-items mixin

The align-items() mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. There is no such CSS property in any IE version (IE10/11 use the standard `align-items` for modern layout, and `-ms-flex-align` for the old syntax, both of which are already emitted). This line is dead code that will be discarded by the CSS parser; it suggests a misunderstanding of the vendor prefix matrix and could mislead future maintainers into relying on it. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: `-ms-align-items` is not a valid CSS property in any version of IE/Edge, and `-ms-flex-align` is the legacy equivalent.

false_positives.candidate:
float rules on children of new flex container are inert

`.small-action` is now a flex container (via `@include flexbox()`), which makes `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270) and `button { float: right; }` (line 309) no-ops: per the flexbox spec, `float` is ignored on flex items. The layout now depends entirely on flex defaults (row, no wrapping, flex-start alignment), so the avatar will sit next to the description and the button will follow it — a visual change that may or may not be intended. Either the float declarations should be deleted as dead code, or explicit flex ordering/alignment (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button) should be added so the button is still pushed to the right edge; currently nothing in the diff guarantees the right-aligned button placement the old float provided.

clear: both has no effect on a flex container

`.small-action` ends with `clear: both;`. With the element now converted to a flex container, `clear` still applies to the container itself as a block-level box, but since the container no longer has floated children (floats on flex items are ignored), the rule serves no purpose and, more importantly, the old clearfix-style guarantee that the small-action box contains its content is now handled differently. If the rule was meant to clear sibling floats (e.g. floated post streams above), it still works, but the comment-free combination of `clear: both` with floats and flexbox on the same element is contradictory and should be cleaned up to make the intended layout mechanism explicit.

Header .title float removed but no flex sizing added; old-webkit-box fallback drops align-items

`.d-header .contents` is now a flex container, and the `.title { float: left; }` rule was deleted. Two concerns: (1) In browsers that pick up the old `-webkit-box` display (older iOS Safari), the `align-items(center)` from the mixin will not apply because `-webkit-box` uses `-webkit-box-align` — that is emitted, but `center` is valid there so alignment is fine; however the `order(3)` on `.panel` is emitted as `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 3`, which old WebKit honors, so ordering is fine — but `margin-left: auto` (the new right-pushing mechanism for `.panel`) is NOT supported as a flex-item auto-margin in the old -webkit-box model, so the panel will not be pushed to the right in those legacy browsers and the login/buttons will sit immediately next to the logo. (2) The old `float: left` on `.title` was the only thing constraining the title block; with flex and no explicit flex-grow, layout is unchanged for modern browsers, but the mixin emits five `display` values, meaning different browsers get different box models while only the modern properties (auto margins) are guaranteed to work in one of them. The legacy `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box`/`-ms-flexbox` fallbacks should either be dropped (Discourse does not target Firefox 21/IE10) or the layout must not depend on auto margins.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper only works if it is a direct flex child

`@include order(2)` was added to `.extra-info-wrapper`. The `order` property only affects flex items, i.e. direct children of a flex container. This works only if `.extra-info-wrapper` is a direct child of `.d-header .contents`. The PR also removed the `margin-top: 5px` compensation for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` inside it while adding `line-height: 1.5` — if `.extra-info-wrapper` is not a direct flex child (or on pages where the header title area renders differently, e.g. topic pages vs. category pages), the `order` is silently ignored and the vertical spacing fix that was removed will not be replaced by flex centering, causing the category bullet badge to sit misaligned. Verify the element hierarchy across all header variants.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix so the guard is never invoked

ActiveModel::Serializers decides whether to include an attribute by calling `include_#{attribute}?` (with a trailing question mark). The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no `?`), so it is never called by the serializer framework. The intended check — only serialize website_name when the website is present — does not run, and website_name is serialized unconditionally (yielding a null key when no website is set, unlike every other guarded attribute in this serializer). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix for ActiveModel::Serializers conditional attribute inclusion. Although it doesn't mention the secondary string concatenation advice, it directly matches the core functional bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 profile data

`website`, `location`, `bio_raw`, etc. are listed in `untrusted_attributes` so they are hidden when a TL0 user is viewed by anonymous visitors (scope.restrict_user_fields?). The new `website_name` attribute is derived directly from `website` but was not added to that list, so the domain/path of a TL0 user's website is serialized to anonymous users even though `website` itself is suppressed. This defeats the existing privacy control. The spec's `untrusted_attributes` list (spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb line 11) also wasn't updated, so the 'doesn't serialize untrusted attributes' test does not cover the new leak.

website_name drops query strings and uses bare rescue on URI parsing

When the domains match, the returned website_name is `host + URI(website).path`, discarding any query string or fragment from the user's URL (e.g. `example.com/page?id=3` becomes `example.com/page`). The PR description says 'show complete URL path', so this silently truncates URLs. Additionally, `URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` swallows all exceptions from malformed URLs; while this returns nil for blanks, a blanket rescue hides unexpected errors — an explicit presence/parse check would be safer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Weak origin check on postMessage handler

The receiver validates messages with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, an unanchored substring test. Any string merely *containing* the discourse origin passes (e.g. an origin like `http://discourse.example.com.attacker.tld` if the forum URL is a substring of it), and the check compares the full URL string against only the origin scheme+host. Use `e.origin === new URL(discourseUrl).origin` for an exact comparison. Impact is limited (message only sets iframe height), but it should be an exact check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation on the message handler uses `indexOf` with `discourseUrl`, which performs an insufficient substring check and can be bypassed by a malicious origin.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Stored XSS: embed URL interpolated unescaped into raw HTML post TopicEmbed.import builds the post body with `contents << "...#{url}..."` without any HTML escaping, and the resulting post is stored with cook_method raw_html (Post#cook returns raw verbatim, bypassing the markdown/sanitization pipeline). The `url` here is the user-supplied `embed_url` request parameter (only checked with a /^https?:\/\// regex), so a URL containing a single quote and a `, is injected into the post body and rendered unsanitized. The embed view renders it with `raw post.cooked`, so any visitor of the embedded page is exposed to stored XSS. The URL must be escaped (CGI.escapeHTML / ERB::Util.html_escape) and ideally validated with URI.parse.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues in the `TopicEmbed.import` method: a `NoMethodError` if `contents` is nil, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped `url` interpolation in the generated HTML. The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same XSS vulnerability due to unescaped `url` interpolation in `TopicEmbed.import`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed crashes when a feed item has no content element

`i.content.scrub` assumes every RSS/Atom item has a `content` element. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements, so any feed item that only provides `description` (or an Atom feed without content) raises NoMethodError on nil. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the whole hourly poll is aborted at the first such item and no further items are imported. Guard with `i.content || i.description` and handle nil.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` can be nil in RSS feeds, and suggests the same fix of falling back to `i.description`.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

The layout embeds `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The controller only validates that the referer's *host* equals embeddable_host; the path/query of the referring URL is attacker-influenced (any page on the embeddable host, or a crafted referer with quotes). A referer containing a single quote or `</script>` breaks out of the JS string literal, allowing script injection into the embed iframe's DOM. Use `escape_javascript`/json encoding for the value instead of raw ERB interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `request.referer` is interpolated directly into inline JavaScript without escaping, leading to an XSS (script injection) vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
create_table with force: true will silently drop an existing table

The migration uses `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`, which issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating. If this migration runs against a database that already has topic_embeds data (e.g. it was created outside migrations, or a partial deploy happened), all rows are silently destroyed. The same problem is introduced in this PR by changing db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb to `force: true`, which can drop production top_topics data on environments where the table already exists. `force: true` should only ever be used in development/test schemas, never in shipped migrations.

Import crashes if the existing embed's post has been deleted

In the update branch, `post = embed.post` may be nil (topic/post deleted by moderators, which is common for spam), and the next line calls `PostRevisor.new(post)` on nil, raising NoMethodError. PollFeed runs hourly and TopicRetriever calls it inline, so a single deleted post for a feed URL permanently breaks feed polling for all items after it (retry disabled). Handle a nil post by recreating the topic or skipping.

No error handling around feed fetch; network error kills scheduled job with retry disabled

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` can raise OpenURI::HTTPError, SocketError, timeouts, or RSS parse errors. With `sidekiq_options retry: false`, any transient network failure silently aborts the poll until the next hour with no logging. Wrap the fetch/parse in begin/rescue with logging so transient errors don't go unnoticed.

Anonymous requests can trigger unauthenticated enqueues of retrieval jobs

Any request passing the referer check (which only checks the host header of the referer, trivially spoofable via server-side fetch or a page on the host) with arbitrary embed_url values enqueues a RetrieveTopic job per unique URL. Although TopicRetriever throttles per-URL to once per 60s, an attacker can rotate unlimited distinct embed_url values (all on the embeddable host), each spawning a job that performs an outbound HTTP fetch (or a full PollFeed run) — a job-queue and outbound-traffic amplification vector with no global rate limit.

import_remote does not restrict scheme, enabling file:// reads

TopicEmbed.import checks `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`, but import_remote calls `open(url)` *before* that check, and Ruby's open-uri follows `file://` (and other schemes via redirects). The embed_url comes from the public controller via the RetrieveTopic job. Although TopicRetriever.invalid_host? compares hosts first, a URL like `file:///etc/passwd` has host nil != embeddable_host and is rejected there; however any code path calling import_remote directly (e.g. the disqus thor task with feed data) passes the URL straight to open(). Use an explicit http(s) check before open(), not just inside import.

feed_key is defined but never used, so polling has no modified/etag check

The job defines `feed_key` (apparently intended for caching feed modified state) but never reads or writes it, and poll_feed re-imports every item on every hourly run, re-fetching and re-parsing each item's page via TopicEmbed.import (dedup is by embed_url, so content changes are re-imported even when the feed hasn't changed). Either wire the key into the polling logic or remove it; as-is it is dead code and the comment-implied caching behavior does not exist.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate downsize definition breaks existing 4-argument callers

The class now defines `downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently overrides the first, so the width/height variant is dead code and any existing caller invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height)` now hits the new signature where `dimensions` receives the width integer and `opts` receives the height integer. The dimensions string passed to convert becomes just the width (e.g. "800" instead of "800x600"), producing a malformed ImageMagick resize argument, and opts is a Fixnum so `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise NoMethodError. All existing thumbnail-generation callers of the old API break at runtime.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (which takes a `dimensions` parameter) to overwrite the first definition (which takes separate width and height parameters), thus breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client limit ignores site settings

The client-side upload validation previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` so it matched the server's per-type configured limits. It now hardcodes 10MB for both images and attachments. On sites configured with smaller limits the client will let a file through that the server then rejects, and on sites with larger attachment limits (e.g. max_attachment_size_kb > 10MB) valid uploads are blocked client-side with a wrong error message. This is a functional regression of the configurable limits.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: hardcoding the 10MB limit (`10 * 1024` KB) ignores `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, causing a mismatch between client-side and server-side per-type limits.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message hardcodes 10MB regardless of server config

The 413 handler now reports "10 MB" as the max size instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When a site has a different max image size configured, the user is shown an incorrect limit in the error dialog, misleading them about what they can upload.

API URL download limit raised to hardcoded 10MB bypassing site setting

The remote-download size cap for API-provided URLs was `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and is now a hardcoded 10.megabytes. This applies to all downloads via the API path (including attachments, not just images that will be downsized), so a site that deliberately lowered max_image_size_kb to limit bandwidth/storage exposure now allows API clients to pull up to 10MB per request from arbitrary URLs, defeating the configured limit.

Downsize loop can silently fail and oversized image still submitted

The loop downsizes to "80%" up to 5 times (max ~33% area reduction) and ignores the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If conversion fails (e.g. ImageMagick error, unsupported format such as SVG or a corrupted image), the loop runs all 5 attempts on an unmodified file and then `Upload.create_for` is called anyway with the still-oversized tempfile. Also, five 20% steps are frequently insufficient for a genuinely large image (e.g. a 40MB photo with a 1MB limit), so the upload will fail with a generic error after the CPU cost of up to 5 image conversions. The downsize result should be checked and a stronger reduction strategy (e.g. scaling toward the target size directly) used.

In-place convert on the same path can corrupt or fail on the source tempfile

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert from[0] ... to` with from == to. ImageMagick reads the input fully before writing, so this usually works, but for animated GIFs the animated path uses gifsicle reading and writing the same file, and any partial write failure leaves the tempfile in a corrupted/truncated state that is then passed to Upload.create_for, potentially producing a broken stored upload. Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original would be safe.

Downsized file keeps original extension/content_type even when format changes

After downsizing, the file is registered via `Upload.create_for(..., filename, ...)` with the original filename and content_type. If ImageMagick's convert writes a different format than the extension suggests (or the animated path produces a different output), the stored upload's extension, content type, and actual bytes can disagree, which can later break thumbnail generation and cause browsers to mis-handle the file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

unsubscribe crashes with nil TopicUser when the user has no topic_user record

For any logged-in user who never viewed/posted/tracked the topic (e.g. they were watching via a category default or received the email via a group mention), no topic_users row exists, so `tu` is nil and the action raises NoMethodError, returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing the user. false_positives.candidate:
State-changing GET endpoint can be triggered by email scanners/link prefetchers

The unsubscribe link in emails is a plain GET to /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe that immediately mutates the user's notification level (topics_controller.rb line 98-116, route added in config/routes.rb line 440-441). Mail clients and security scanners (antivirus proxies, Gmail link scanning, Apple Mail prefetch) routinely GET links in emails without the user clicking them. Any such scan silently mutes the user's topic, or worse toggles them to regular, without consent. Standard practice (and what the existing /email/unsubscribe/:key flow does) is a token-authenticated link or a confirmation page; this endpoint requires only a logged-in session and a guessable numeric topic id, and it also lets any logged-in user flip their own state via CSRF-free GET from any page (img tag on any site they visit while logged in, since there is no CSRF check on GET).

The unsubscribe action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of going through `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is the canonical path: it sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (so the UI shows why the level changed) and publishes a `notification_level_change` MessageBus message to /topic/:id so open tabs update. Saving directly leaves the reason stale (e.g. still 'auto_watch') and other clients' UIs out of sync. Also, an unsubscribe click when the level is 'regular' or below sets it to 'muted', but when it is 'tracking'/'watching' it only drops to 'regular' — a 'regular' user still receives replied-to/mentioned notifications for that topic, so the email's promise 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here' (config/locales/server.en.yml) is not kept for those users.

Cancellation query does not filter by method EMAIL, so SendGrid is called with Twilio SIDs

If a non-email (SMS) reminder row ever ends up with `cancelled: true`, the loop will POST its Twilio message SID to the SendGrid `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` endpoint as a `batch_id`. That request fails, the thrown error is caught by the surrounding try/catch which aborts the whole loop, and all remaining email reminders in the batch are left uncancelled (and their DB rows undeleted) for that run. Each reminder should be cancelled/deleted individually with per-reminder error handling, and the query should filter `method: EMAIL`.

Cancellation only happens within 1 hour of the scheduled date, allowing late cron runs to miss emails

Reminders are only cancelled once `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, and the cron runs every 15 minutes. A booking cancelled shortly before a reminder's scheduled date (e.g. 10 minutes before) will only be processed at the next cron tick, which can be after the email has already been sent by SendGrid. There is no compensation for this window (e.g. cancelling immediately when the request comes in, or SendGrid-side suppression), so the original bug ('cancelled bookings still receive reminders') persists for reminders close to their send time.

If Twilio cancelSMS fails the reminder row is not deleted and never retried

In `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`, if `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` throws, the subsequent `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` is skipped (the catch swallows the error). The row survives with its referenceId, but nothing ever retries the cancellation — the callers have already moved on — so the SMS is still sent for a cancelled/rescheduled booking. The Twilio cancel and the DB delete should be decoupled so a Twilio failure doesn't prevent cleanup, or the row should be marked for retry like the email path.

Cancellation loop aborts entirely on the first SendGrid failure

The per-reminder SendGrid cancel request is inside a single try/catch wrapping the whole loop. One failing request (e.g. a stale/invalid batch_id for a reminder whose email was already sent) throws, skips the DB delete for that reminder and skips cancelling every subsequent reminder in `remindersToCancel` for this run; the failed reminder will fail again on every future run, permanently blocking the rest of the queue. Each reminder should be cancelled and deleted inside its own try/catch.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup code list is read from the DB, matched, set to null, and written back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code can be replayed and used twice (or more). The update should be conditional/atomic (e.g., compare-and-set in a transaction, or store per-code hash and delete with a WHERE clause that asserts the code still exists).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same race condition where backup codes are read, modified in memory, and written back non-atomically, allowing concurrent login requests to reuse the same single-use backup code.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code is consumed before the login flow completes

The verified backup code is deleted and the DB updated inside authorize(), before next-auth issues the session/JWT and before the signIn callback runs. If anything downstream fails (signIn callback error, network failure on the client, next-auth internal error), the user's backup code is permanently burned without a successful login, reducing their remaining recovery codes through no fault of their own. Ideally consumption should happen only once login is certain to succeed.

Backup codes unusable for third-party identity provider (SAML/Google) 2FA users

The check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` runs before the backup code branch. Users whose accounts use SAML/Google identity but have 2FA enabled (the totp-link login path) can never authenticate with a backup code: submitting a backupCode without a totpCode always throws, and the login page's 'Lost access' backup-code UI is not offered on the totpEmail path either. These users have no recovery option if they lose their authenticator, despite the feature claiming to provide one.

No test for the core feature: logging in with a backup code

The PR adds backup-code login and backup-code-based 2FA disable, but the only new test coverage clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (and even that doesn't verify file or clipboard content). There is no test that a user can actually log in with a backup code, that a used code is rejected on reuse, that an incorrect code shows the right error, or that disabling 2FA with a backup code works — all explicitly deferred as TODOs. The primary security-relevant code path ships untested.

Both totpCode and backupCode can be submitted; backup code silently takes precedence

When switching between the TOTP and 'Lost access' backup-code views, only one field is cleared in some transitions, and onSubmit spreads all form values into signIn(). The authorize() handler checks backupCode first, so a user who has a stale backupCode value in the form while trying to log in with a TOTP code will get an 'incorrect backup code' error (or worse, succeed via a leftover backup code) even though they typed a valid TOTP. The submit should send only the code relevant to the currently active mode.

Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled

The setup endpoint writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row on every call, even if the user never completes the enable step. A user who starts setup, sees/saves codes, then restarts setup later and completes only the second attempt will have the first set of saved codes silently invalidated (overwritten). Also, codes exist on the DB for users who never enabled 2FA. Generating/persisting codes only on successful enable (or returning them from enable) would make the displayed codes authoritative.

Crash when destinationCalendar is null: mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration on undefined

In EventManager.create(), `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields undefined when destinationCalendar is null/undefined, and the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining (`evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`). The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was null-safe. Any booking where destinationCalendar is null and location is Google Meet (e.g. handleNewBooking now explicitly sets destinationCalendar to null when neither eventType nor organizer has one) will throw a TypeError and abort booking creation.

Organizer email forced to first host's destination calendar externalId even when event is created under a different host's credential

In createEvent (and updateEvent), the organizer attendee's email is overridden with `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId` — always the FIRST entry of destinationCalendar — regardless of which credential/selectedCalendar the event is actually created on. In a collective event with multiple hosts, when EventManager iterates the second host's destination calendar (different credentialId), the event is created on the second host's calendar but the organizer email still points at the first host's calendar externalId. This produces events attributed to the wrong organizer, can break Google Meet conference creation tied to the organizer, and causes mismatched organizer identity across hosts' calendars.

createEvent silently falls back to "primary" when destinationCalendar has no entry for this credential

`calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"` means that when destinationCalendar is non-empty but none of its entries has a matching credentialId (e.g. credential not in the list, or a stale destinationCalendar pointing at a removed credential), the event is silently created on the current credential's primary calendar instead of the intended destination. Combined with the 404-is-swallowed behavior in CalendarManager.createEvent, this can create duplicate/misplaced events on the wrong calendar with no error surfaced. It should log/skip when an explicit destination was requested but not found for this credential.

CalDAV createEvent only honors the first destinationCalendar, so collective multi-host events are not created on other hosts' calendars

BaseCalendarService.createEvent destructures only `[mainHostDestinationCalendar]` and filters calendars by that single externalId. Since EventManager now iterates all destinationCalendar entries and calls createEvent once per credential, a second host using a CalDAV-based calendar (Apple/iCloud/etc.) will have their event filtered out because their destination's externalId is never compared — only the first host's externalId is. The multi-host fix therefore does not work for CalDAV integrations; the filter should check whether any destinationCalendar entry matches the calendar, or the service should receive the specific destination being targeted.

Only the first destinationCalendar is persisted on the booking row, losing other hosts' calendars for later operations

When creating the booking record, the prisma connect uses `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` only. For collective events where evt.destinationCalendar contains multiple hosts' destination calendars, only the organizer's is connected to the Booking. Any code path that reconstructs the CalendarEvent from the booking without consulting references (e.g. requestReschedule, cancel fallbacks, reminders, payment webhooks) will therefore only see one destination calendar. The per-credential booking references partially compensate, but the persisted booking.destinationCalendar no longer reflects the event's full set of destination calendars.

loadUsers rewrite changes error behavior and drops organization selection for dynamic bookings

The rewritten loadUsers no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` for dynamic (non-eventType) bookings, so downstream code that relied on user.organization.slug for dynamic group bookings will now get undefined. Additionally, the new try/catch converts ordinary errors into a generic 500 "Unable to load users" and wraps Prisma known-request errors as 400s, changing the API error contract for dynamic bookings. These changes are incidental to the PR's purpose and untested.

destinationCalendar payload shape changed from null/object to array — breaking change for webhook consumers

The e2e snapshot updates show `destinationCalendar` in webhook payloads changing from `null` (or a single object) to `[]`/array of objects. This is an outward-facing breaking change to the BOOKING_* webhook payload contract that external integrations depend on; existing consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` or check `=== null` will break. The PR is labeled "non-breaking bug fix" but this is a public API contract change with no migration note or versioning.

In the allRemainingBookings branch inside the per-reference loop, deletion of updated bookings iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(type.endsWith("_calendar"))` rather than the reference's credentialId, and uses only the first calendar reference per updated booking (`updBooking.references.find(...)`). In createAllCalendarEvents' else branch (no destinationCalendar), the fallback filters `this.calendarCredentials.filter((cred) => cred.type === "calendar")`. No credential in the system has type exactly "calendar" (types are google_calendar, office365_calendar, etc.), so this fallback finds nothing and no calendar event is created at all. It should filter by type.endsWith("_calendar") (excluding other_calendar) or pick the first calendar credential, as the old code effectively did via destinationCalendar.

No tests added for the multi-destinationCalendar collective booking behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The core change (destinationCalendar becoming an array, per-credential event creation for collective events, multi-reference update/cancel paths in EventManager and handleCancelBooking) is a substantial behavioral change affecting booking creation, reschedule, cancel, and payment webhooks, with several risky code paths (null destinationCalendar, fallback branches). At minimum, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents/updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations and a null destinationCalendar case are needed before merging.

forEach(async ...) swallows the returned promises, so deletions are unawaited and errors escape the try/catch

The loop `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` discards the promises returned by the async callbacks. Because the callback is now async (it was made async by this PR to await getCalendar), the surrounding try/catch can no longer catch errors thrown while resolving the app import or getCalendar — any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and Reschedule() can return before calendar/video events are actually deleted. false_positives.candidate:
Restarting a 'hung' process can run two flushers on the same shards, producing duplicate segments

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), `process.kill()` is called and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards`. `kill()` is asynchronous — the old process can still be inside its flush loop while the new process starts flushing the same shards. Both processes can call `buffer.flush_segments()` and produce the same segments to Kafka before either calls `done_flush_segments`, resulting in duplicate segments in the buffered-segments topic (duplicate span data downstream). The old process is also never joined, so it is never confirmed dead before the replacement starts. The replacement should only be started after the old process has actually exited (join with timeout), and ideally after verifying no in-flight flush.

Thread-based flusher (produce_to_pipe path) is never killed on restart, so restarts stack threads

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, the flusher 'process' is a `threading.Thread`. On an unhealthy restart, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so the old thread is left running and a new one is spawned for the same shards. A hung thread never recovers, so every restart adds another thread; if the hang is caused by a stuck `produce` (as in the backpressure test, where append sleeps), multiple threads will flush the same shards concurrently, duplicating messages. This mostly affects the test path today, but the code claims Thread support, so it should either kill/stop the old thread cooperatively (e.g. per-process stop flag) or refuse to restart thread-based flushers.

Restart counter never resets, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer even if each process is healthy

`process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented; there is no reset after a process proves itself healthy. With MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10, a shard-group that legitimately restarts 11 times over the entire lifetime of a long-running consumer (e.g. due to transient Redis/Kafka failures hours apart) will trigger `RuntimeError` and crash the whole consumer, taking down all shard flushers. The counter should reset (or decay) after a period of healthy operation, as was the case before this change for the single process — but this PR now makes it much more likely since a single misbehaving shard-group among many takes the consumer down.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` with a process index directly). It also has a bug if it were used: it would overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous process. It should be removed.

No test that multiple flusher processes actually flush their shards end-to-end

The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts process/shard bookkeeping (counts and map sizes); it never submits a span or asserts that a segment is produced. There is no test covering the core new behavior: that with multiple flusher processes, spans on shards assigned to different processes are all flushed exactly once, nor a test for the restart path (`_ensure_processes_alive` with multiple processes), which is where the trickiest new logic lives. A regression in shard-to-process mapping or in restart handling would pass the current test suite.

submit() iterates self.buffers while restarts mutate it

`submit()` and `_ensure_processes_alive()` run on the main thread, so the dict mutation itself is not racy in-process. However `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.buffers[process_index]` with a brand new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each restart. If a restart happens between the `record_stored_segments()` loop and the memory-info loop within a single `submit()` call, some shards' buffers get recorded twice and some not at all within that call; more importantly each restart allocates a new SpansBuffer (with new Redis clients) while old ones are never closed, leaking Redis connections over repeated restarts.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Federated recovery-code credential is never removed and codes are never consumed

This means the security of the codes (hashing vs. plaintext storage) is delegated entirely to third-party storage implementations, whereas the local provider always stores only hashes. Additionally, the fully-populated credentialModel with hashed codes that the caller built is discarded in this branch, so the provider loses the createdDate/userLabel metadata.
