true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds and lost index writes

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its whole duration, which (despite the perf cost) guaranteed only one index per NamespacedResource was ever built and published to the cache. Now the lock is only taken around `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two callers can build the same key concurrently: during `searchSupport.init` (multi-worker errgroup) and via `getOrCreateIndex` triggered by a watch event or a Search request arriving while init is still building. Consequences: (1) two bleveIndex objects exist for the same key; the loser of the last cache write keeps getting writes (e.g. from handleEvent) into an index that is no longer in the cache, so those documents silently vanish from search results — data loss for the index; (2) for file-backed indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both builds call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, which will fail (index already exists) or corrupt the on-disk index. getOrCreateIndex's own TODO comment ("we don't want to block while anything is building, just the same key") confirms per-key serialization is required; this change removed even the coarse serialization without adding a per-key one.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: moving b.cacheMu from protecting all of BuildIndex to only the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to build the same expensive index for the same key concurrently. Its additional claimed consequences do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now performs full index build synchronously, changing the constructor contract for all callers

Init() (which builds the entire search index over all namespaces and can take a long time on large installations) is now invoked inside NewResourceServer, and any init failure makes the constructor return an error. Previously, callers such as embedded/in-process usage of the resource server (e.g. apiserver storage wiring, tests, single-binary Grafana where the unified storage may be created alongside other services) got a server immediately and initialization happened lazily or in the background. Those callers now block startup for the whole index build and will fail hard if the index build errors (e.g. transient DB issue during startup), where previously reads/writes could still be served. The PR description itself flags this ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") — the callers of NewResourceServer outside the storage-server target need to be audited; no such audit or feature flag is included.

Failed Init in constructor leaks the server's background context and goroutines

When s.Init(ctx) fails inside NewResourceServer, the function returns nil, err, but s.cancel() is never called. Init may have already started background work before failing — notably searchSupport.init's watch-event goroutine (started after WatchWriteEvents succeeds) and the lifecycle hooks' partial initialization. With no reference to the server retained by the caller, those goroutines and the cancelable context are leaked for the life of the process. The error path should call s.cancel() (or s.Stop) before returning.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in init's worker goroutines

In searchSupport.init, the loop over stats spawns goroutines (limited by initWorkers, so several run concurrently) that both execute `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assign `_, _, err = s.build(...)` where `err` is the outer function-scope variable declared at `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`. These are unsynchronized concurrent read/writes of shared variables — a data race under Go's memory model (and `go test -race` will flag it), and the shared `err` can be clobbered by a later goroutine, causing a real build error to be lost so init reports success with a missing index. Each goroutine should use its own local counter/err (e.g. `i, e := 0, error(nil)` captured per closure), with totals aggregated after group.Wait().

Watch event goroutine has no termination path and panics on closed channel

The goroutine started at the end of init reads `v := <-events` in an infinite loop with no select on a done channel. When the storage backend closes the events channel (e.g. the SQL poller exits when b.done fires on Stop, which closes the stream), the receive yields nil forever and s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) dereferences evt.Type/evt.Key, panicking the process. Additionally, because this uses context.Background(), there is no way to stop it on shutdown. Now that init runs in the constructor for the storage-server target, every server start creates this goroutine, so it must be tied to the server's cancelable context.

Init ordering change: watch events consumed by searchSupport.init but broadcaster started after — event gap risk and misordering rationale

The diff moves initWatcher() to after s.search.init(). searchSupport.init internally starts its own WatchWriteEvents subscription, so this ordering is intentional (watch events are captured while the index builds). However, the server's broadcaster (used by the Watch RPC) is only started after the potentially long index build completes. During that window, Watch RPCs that do reach the server (the gRPC server may already be serving since the module server registers services before/around construction) will fail or block on s.broadcaster — notably s.broadcaster is nil until initWatcher succeeds, so a Watch call during init will nil-pointer panic on `s.broadcaster.Subscribe`. At minimum the nil broadcaster needs a guard, or initWatcher should run before search init (with search's own event subscription providing continuity, which is the pre-existing design).

Storage-server integration test disabled for postgres with no follow-up issue

The only integration test covering the storage-server target (which is exactly the code path changed by this PR — eager init of unified storage at startup) is now skipped for postgres with a TODO comment ("not working with postgres in Drone"). This means the main behavioral change in this PR (synchronous index init at startup) has no integration coverage on one of the two supported databases, and the failure cause is neither diagnosed nor tracked. Since this test is the regression guard for the change, the skip should be replaced by a fix or linked to a tracked issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, giving at-most-once semantics

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, exceptions from result_processor are caught and only logged (line 144-147), and the finally block at line 149 always calls offset_tracker.complete_offset. The offset is then treated as processed and will be committed by the commit loop. Combined with ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 53-54) which also swallows all exceptions, any transient failure (e.g. a DB error while handling a result) silently drops the message and advances the committed offset past it, so the message is never retried. This contradicts the class docstring's guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and turns the consumer into an at-most-once pipeline with silent data loss.

close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, breaking rebalance recovery

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. The queue_pool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

Background commit thread commits without regard to partition ownership

The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

--max-workers help text/semantics conflate worker threads and queue count

In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. Consider documenting the remapping caveat and the differing default.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache reintroduces the 'cannot access newly created resource' bug the PR fixes

The permDenialCache entry for (namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder) is set with a 30s TTL whenever a Check is denied, and any later Check with the same key short-circuits to denied before the permission cache or DB is consulted (service.go:116-121). Consider the exact scenario the PR describes: a user without a scoped permission triggers a Check for e.g. dashboards:read on name 'newdash' in folder 'fold1' (e.g. a pre-flight check, a duplicate-name check, or a failed attempt), which populates a denial entry. The user then creates the dashboard/folder, which writes the permission row to the DB. The next Check for that same (user, action, name, folder) hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false without ever re-querying the DB — so the creator is still locked out of their newly created resource for up to 30 seconds. Any mechanism that invalidates/refreshes permCache (e.g. a DB requery triggered by a different resource name) does not invalidate the denial entry, so the denial can even outlive a freshly queried permission map that would allow the request. The denial cache needs to be invalidated when permissions change (e.g. on permission/role writes or resource creation), or its scope/TTL must be bounded so it cannot mask fresh grants.

Denial cache key uses the raw subject identifier, not the resolved user UID

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID (the raw ID parsed from the subject string), whereas the permission cache key (userPermCacheKey) is built from the resolved userIdentifiers.UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:360, 379). Since GetUserIdentifiers accepts both numeric user IDs and UIDs as the subject identifier (service.go:463-469), the same user can be addressed as 'user:112' or 'user:<uid>'. The denial decision was computed from the resolved identity's permissions, but it is stored under the caller-supplied identifier. Consequences: (1) denial entries are not shared between the two spellings, causing unnecessary duplicate DB requeries; (2) if the mapping between a numeric ID and UID ever changes (user deletion/recreation), a stale denial entry keyed by the numeric ID remains valid and keeps denying the new identity for up to 30s. The key should use the resolved UID, consistent with the permission cache.

Denial-cache hits are counted as permission-cache hits in metrics

When the denial cache short-circuits a Check, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit). This conflates the new denial cache with the permission cache, making the permissionCacheUsage metric misleading for operators tuning cache behavior: a denial hit is reported as a permission cache hit even though the permission cache was never consulted. A separate label or metric (e.g. permissionDenialCacheUsage) should be used.

No test covers the denial cache being populated by a denied Check and its interaction with later allowed checks

The only denial-cache test ('Should deny on explicit cache deny entry') manually pre-populates permDenialCache; there is no test that a Check returning Allowed=false actually writes a denial entry and that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits without touching the store. More importantly, there is no test for the interaction the feature exists for: after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant of the permission in the store (simulating resource creation) — the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sibling case where permCache/DB allow but the denial entry denies. Without such a test the stale-denial regression risk (denial entry masking a fresh DB allow) is unguarded.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No cache recheck after acquiring the write lock (missing double-checked locking)

After the RLock fast path fails, GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock and unconditionally re-reads the manifest from disk/CDN and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache. If N concurrent requests arrive before the cache is populated (e.g. at startup in non-Dev mode), every one of them performs the file read serially instead of one goroutine populating the cache and the rest reusing it. The fix is incomplete double-checked locking: after taking the write lock, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it if non-nil (for the non-Dev case).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache recheck after GetWebAssets acquires the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate a cache already filled by another goroutine.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across file I/O and CDN HTTP request

GetWebAssets holds entryPointAssetsCacheMu (write lock) for the entire duration of readWebAssetsFromFile and, if a CDN URL is ever set, the blocking HTTP request in readWebAssetsFromCDN (currently the cdn variable is hardcoded to "", but that is an existing call path). In Dev mode this happens on every call. A slow or hanging CDN request would block every other caller of GetWebAssets, including the RLock fast-path readers, stalling request handling. Consider loading the result outside the lock and only taking the lock briefly to publish it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are canceled when the request context ends

In Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). As soon as the API request returns, the request context is canceled, so the deferred legacy write/delete is aborted with 'context canceled' rather than running for its timeout. This defeats the stated purpose of the mode ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or background) as the parent.

DeleteCollection records legacy result with the storage metrics recorder

In DeleteCollection's goroutine, the outcome of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latencies and failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics used to monitor migration progress.

Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy metrics

When d.Storage.Create fails (line 45) or d.Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the legacy store was never contacted. These failures and their durations are attributed to legacy storage, skewing the dual-writer observability data. Both should be recordStorageDuration.

Legacy write failures are swallowed with no logging or reconciliation

Previously, errors from the legacy store were at least logged. In the new goroutines, the error from d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is only converted into a boolean for a metric; it is never logged and no reconciliation/retry is queued. Since mode 3 is the last dual-write stage before cutting over to unified storage, silent legacy failures mean data loss in the legacy store with no operator-visible signal beyond an aggregate counter and no way to recover the missed write.

Legacy Update reuses the request's objInfo, so legacy can write different data than storage

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so the legacy store received exactly the object that unified storage wrote (via updateWrapper). The new code passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update in a goroutine, so the legacy store re-computes the updated object from its own (possibly stale) current state. If legacy and unified have diverged (e.g., an earlier async legacy write was canceled or failed), the legacy copy can end up with different content than the authoritative unified copy. The updateWrapper mechanism was removed without a replacement guarantee.

Legacy Delete failures on NotFound are treated as errors

The old Delete tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy store (expected when an object exists only in unified storage, which is the common case in mode 3 after migration backfill gaps). The new code records any legacy Delete error, including NotFound, as a failure metric. In mode 3, objects created before backfill will routinely 404 in legacy, producing persistent false failure signals.

Unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens

Mode 3's defining behavior is 'write to unified, then asynchronously write to legacy', but none of the tests assert that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are invoked (e.g., via m.AssertExpectations or waiting on the goroutine with mock.AssertEventually). The tests return immediately after the unified call, so the goroutines may not have run; a regression that drops the legacy write entirely (or is canceled immediately, as in the context bug) would still pass. Also the error-path test cases set up legacy mock expectations that are never exercised or verified.

TestMode3_Get creates its own registry instead of the shared one

TestMode3_Get declares a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while every other mode-3 test uses the package-level `p`. This is inconsistent and, if the dual writer registers metrics in NewDualWriter, would panic on double registration in other tests or mask registration issues; the unrelated change to TestMode1_Get that moved `p` to package scope suggests this local declaration is an oversight.

The deleted GrafanaRuleLoader built the list-item href with `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo })` so navigating to a rule from the list and back preserved the list context. `[canPause, canSilence, shouldShowDeclareIncidentButton, canDuplicate].some(Boolean) && [canExport].some(Boolean)` — the second clause is equivalent to plain `canExport`. Beyond style, this makes the divider logic hard to verify and suggests an intended condition that was never written (e.g. shareUrl should probably also gate the divider, otherwise 'Copy link' can appear directly above/below a divider inconsistently when canExport is false). Simplify to an explicit expression.

getGrafanaRuleKey emits a stray '}' in the generated key

The template literal ends with `${rule.uid}}`, adding a literal closing brace to every grafana rule key. Harmless for uniqueness today but it is a typo that will confuse anyone extending the key format, and since this key mechanism was just re-wired (and is the key that should be passed to GrafanaRuleListItem per the missing-key finding), fix the stray character.

Interpolating before the $__range guard defeats the no-split check for range-variable queries

runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on each target before the partition step. The subsequent querySupportsSplitting() check relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) detecting a literal $__range/$__range_s variables in the expression (see the comment at querySplitting.ts:285-287: queries with $__range must not be split because the backend interpolates $__range against the split sub-range). After applyTemplateVariables runs, $__range has already been replaced with the full original time range, so isQueryWithRangeVariable never matches and such queries are now split into per-day chunks with the full-range value baked into the expr. Every sub-request then aggregates over the whole range instead of its chunk, producing duplicated/incorrect data for any query using $__range. The interpolation must happen after the range-variable check, or the check must run on the pre-interpolation expression.

Double template interpolation in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables(), but the resulting queries are then passed to runSplitQuery(), which (after this PR) calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on the same targets (querySplitting.ts:299). Template interpolation is not idempotent in general: if a variable's value itself contains text that looks like a variable reference or a `$` character (common in label-filter values, regex patterns, or chained variables), the second pass will re-interpolate the already-substituted value and corrupt the expression or step. Either runShardSplitQuery should skip interpolation and let runSplitQuery do it once, or runSplitQuery needs a way to know the targets are already interpolated. There is also no test covering this double-interpolation scenario.

$__auto and other interval macros are frozen to the full-range value across all split chunks

By interpolating with datasource.applyTemplateVariables before splitting, built-in macros like $__auto (and any interval-derived variable) are resolved once against the original request's range/interval and then reused verbatim in every sub-request's narrower time range. Previously the backend resolved these per sub-request, allowing each chunk to use a range-appropriate value. The new test in querySplitting.test.ts ('Interpolates queries before execution') hard-codes the expectation that $__auto becomes 5m for all three daily chunks, which codifies the behavior change; for range-sensitive macros this can change results (e.g., count_over_time windows no longer adapting per chunk). This should be confirmed as intended and, if so, documented, since it silently changes query semantics for existing dashboards.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices in one session and, if the count is below deviceLimit, performs the insert in a separate session/transaction. Two (or many) concurrent requests from different new devices can each observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-insert must be atomic (e.g. a single conditional insert/transaction with a lock, or a unique count constraint) to actually enforce the limit under load, which is exactly the scenario (burst of anonymous requests) this feature targets.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same count-then-insert race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and collectively exceed the limit. Both recommend making the check and insertion atomic using a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ErrDeviceLimitReached returned raw from Authenticate produces an opaque 500-style auth failure

When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns that error directly. The authn layer will treat this as an internal authentication error rather than an expected 'too many devices' condition, so users over the limit will get a generic error (likely 500 Internal Server Error on every request) with no indication of the cause. There is no mapping of this sentinel error to an appropriate HTTP status (e.g. 403/429) or user-facing message anywhere in this PR, making the feature effectively brick anonymous access without explanation once the limit is hit (combined with the cache bug, intermittently).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that returning ErrDeviceLimitReached from TagDevice directly causes Authenticate to fail, blocking anonymous access when the device limit is reached. The candidate additionally discusses error presentation, but explicitly identifies the same authentication-blocking behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Expiry window logic: a device that exists but is older than 30 days can never be updated when limit is reached, and error semantics conflate cases

updateDevice's WHERE clause requires updated_at BETWEEN (UpdatedAt-30d) and (UpdatedAt+1m). If the count of active devices has reached the limit but the requesting device's row exists yet falls outside that window (e.g. clock skew or a device idle just past 30 days before cleanup runs), the UPDATE affects 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached even though this device is one of the 'expired' rows that shouldn't count toward the limit. The store then neither updates nor deletes the stale row, so the device stays locked out until the 61-day cleanup job removes it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same error-semantics bug: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when the UPDATE affects zero rows because the device falls outside the timestamp window, rather than because a device limit was reached. Its additional lockout discussion does not change that match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed after the first rejected request due to localCache set before the DB call

In tagDeviceUI, localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) is executed before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device ID is still marked as tagged in the 29-minute local cache. On the user's next request, the cache hit makes tagDeviceUI return nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. The net effect is that the device limit only rejects each new device once per ~29 minutes; every subsequent request from that device authenticates successfully. The cache entry must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (and any error path should invalidate it).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry cached on ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
TagDevice moved onto the synchronous request path, removing the previous timeout/async isolation

The old code ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute context.WithTimeout, so database slowness in the anon_device table never delayed or failed anonymous authentication. The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously inside Authenticate using the request context. Now every anonymous request performs up to two extra DB round trips (COUNT + INSERT/UPDATE) before the identity is returned; a slow or locked anon_device table will hang or fail all anonymous access. If the synchronous behavior is required to surface the limit error, consider at minimum retaining a timeout so DB issues cannot degrade anonymous auth.

AnonymousDeviceLimit exposed to all frontend clients including anonymous users

AnonymousDeviceLimit is included in the frontend settings DTO served to every requester, including unauthenticated/anonymous visitors. This leaks an instance's configured capacity limit (useful reconnaissance for abuse: an attacker knows exactly how many spoofed X-Grafana-Device-Id values are needed to lock out legitimate anonymous users, since the limit is enforced per arbitrary client-supplied device IDs). Consider only exposing it to signed-in admins, or not exposing it at all if no frontend code consumes it — no frontend usage is added in this PR, only the type declarations.

New device_limit setting is undocumented and lacks validation

The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting is parsed with MustInt64(0) but has no documentation (configure docs/conf defaults), and negative values are not rejected. A negative value behaves like 0 (limit disabled) due to the `deviceLimit > 0` check, silently ignoring the user's intent; a validation error for negative values would be clearer. Also note that device_limit interacts with the 61-day retention (keepFor) in impl.go while the limit counts only devices active in the last 30 days — this asymmetry is nowhere documented for operators.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are never loaded outside of the ApplicationController#set_locale path

I18n.translate loads only `config.locale` (line 68) before delegating to the real translate, which will now walk the fallback chain defined by FallbackLocaleList (user locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en). The fallback locales are only pre-loaded via ApplicationController#set_locale's `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call. Any translation performed outside a web request — background jobs (Sidekiq), mailers, rake tasks, one-off scripts — will look up keys in fallback locales that were never loaded, so the Fallbacks backend will return 'translation missing' strings instead of the English/default text. The accelerator should ensure all fallback locales for the current locale are loaded inside `translate`/`load_locale`, not rely on the controller filter.

The cache key is built from `key`, `config.locale` and the backend object id. With this PR the effective translation for a given I18n.locale also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (via FallbackLocaleList#[]). When an admin changes default_locale at runtime, the fallback order changes but the cache key does not, so previously cached results from the old fallback chain keep being served for up to LRU_CACHE_SIZE (300) entries until they age out. There is no I18n.reload!/cache invalidation hooked to the default_locale SiteSetting in this change, so users in a non-default locale will continue seeing translations from the old default locale. The key should incorporate the fallback locales (or the cache should be cleared when default_locale changes).

FallbackLocaleList is a Hash whose lookup semantics are entirely in `[]`, with no stored entries. Any code in the i18n gem, Rails, or plugins that interacts with `I18n.fallbacks` through Hash methods other than `[]` (e.g. `each`, `key?`, `keys`, `merge!`, `store`) will see an empty hash: per-locale fallback rules configured that way are silently dropped, and any code that iterates the fallbacks map (for preloading, validation, or locale resolution) will do nothing. Subclassing Hash while making `[]` lie about the contents is fragile; a plain object responding to `[]` (and to whatever the i18n version in use requires) would be safer, or the entries should actually be stored in the hash.

Fallback lookup dereferences SiteSetting.default_locale on every translation, which is not safe during boot or before SiteSetting is available

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every translation lookup. During application boot (initializers, eager loading, asset precompilation) or in contexts where the settings table/connection is not available, SiteSetting may raise or return nil; `nil.to_sym` yields a symbol that then goes through the load path and could trigger DB queries or errors at times when translations are used before the app is fully initialized. A safer approach is to memoize the fallback list and only refresh it when the setting actually changes, and to guard against SiteSetting being unavailable.

The comment at the top states the file must load after 02-freedom_patches.rb, and this happens to work because Rails loads initializers alphabetically and digits sort before letters. But the i18n initializer's `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` must apply to the backend class before it is used, and the pluralization include replaces the removed config/initializers/pluralization.rb — whose old filename sorted before i18n.rb, so any load-order dependent behavior (e.g. plugins or freedom patches touching I18n) silently depends on string sort order. If anyone renames this file (e.g. to `20-i18n.rb` or adds a locale-related initializer), the ordering requirement breaks with no error. The dependency should be explicit (require the freedom patch file, or use config.initializer with `before`/`after`), not a comment.

This line is dead code that will be discarded by the CSS parser; it suggests a misunderstanding of the vendor prefix matrix and could mislead future maintainers into relying on it. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify -ms-align-items as a nonexistent legacy CSS property and identify -ms-flex-align as the correct alternative. The candidate addresses the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
float rules on children of new flex container are inert

`.small-action` is now a flex container (via `@include flexbox()`), which makes `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270) and `button { float: right; }` (line 309) no-ops: per the flexbox spec, `float` is ignored on flex items. The layout now depends entirely on flex defaults (row, no wrapping, flex-start alignment), so the avatar will sit next to the description and the button will follow it — a visual change that may or may not be intended. Either the float declarations should be deleted as dead code, or explicit flex ordering/alignment (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button) should be added so the button is still pushed to the right edge; currently nothing in the diff guarantees the right-aligned button placement the old float provided.

clear: both has no effect on a flex container

`.small-action` ends with `clear: both;`. With the element now converted to a flex container, `clear` still applies to the container itself as a block-level box, but since the container no longer has floated children (floats on flex items are ignored), the rule serves no purpose and, more importantly, the old clearfix-style guarantee that the small-action box contains its content is now handled differently. If the rule was meant to clear sibling floats (e.g. floated post streams above), it still works, but the comment-free combination of `clear: both` with floats and flexbox on the same element is contradictory and should be cleaned up to make the intended layout mechanism explicit.

Header .title float removed but no flex sizing added; old-webkit-box fallback drops align-items

`.d-header .contents` is now a flex container, and the `.title { float: left; }` rule was deleted. Two concerns: (1) In browsers that pick up the old `-webkit-box` display (older iOS Safari), the `align-items(center)` from the mixin will not apply because `-webkit-box` uses `-webkit-box-align` — that is emitted, but `center` is valid there so alignment is fine; however the `order(3)` on `.panel` is emitted as `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 3`, which old WebKit honors, so ordering is fine — but `margin-left: auto` (the new right-pushing mechanism for `.panel`) is NOT supported as a flex-item auto-margin in the old -webkit-box model, so the panel will not be pushed to the right in those legacy browsers and the login/buttons will sit immediately next to the logo. (2) The old `float: left` on `.title` was the only thing constraining the title block; with flex and no explicit flex-grow, layout is unchanged for modern browsers, but the mixin emits five `display` values, meaning different browsers get different box models while only the modern properties (auto margins) are guaranteed to work in one of them. The legacy `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box`/`-ms-flexbox` fallbacks should either be dropped (Discourse does not target Firefox 21/IE10) or the layout must not depend on auto margins.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper only works if it is a direct flex child

`@include order(2)` was added to `.extra-info-wrapper`. The `order` property only affects flex items, i.e. direct children of a flex container. This works only if `.extra-info-wrapper` is a direct child of `.d-header .contents`. The PR also removed the `margin-top: 5px` compensation for `.badge-wrapper.bullet` inside it while adding `line-height: 1.5` — if `.extra-info-wrapper` is not a direct flex child (or on pages where the header title area renders differently, e.g. topic pages vs. category pages), the `order` is silently ignored and the vertical spacing fix that was removed will not be replaced by flex centering, causing the category bullet badge to sit misaligned. Verify the element hierarchy across all header variants.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix so the guard is never invoked

ActiveModel::Serializers decides whether to include an attribute by calling `include_#{attribute}?` (with a trailing question mark). The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no `?`), so it is never called by the serializer framework. The intended check — only serialize website_name when the website is present — does not run, and website_name is serialized unconditionally (yielding a null key when no website is set, unlike every other guarded attribute in this serializer). Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its impact on conditional serialization. It omits the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 profile data

`website`, `location`, `bio_raw`, etc. are listed in `untrusted_attributes` so they are hidden when a TL0 user is viewed by anonymous visitors (scope.restrict_user_fields?). The new `website_name` attribute is derived directly from `website` but was not added to that list, so the domain/path of a TL0 user's website is serialized to anonymous users even though `website` itself is suppressed. This defeats the existing privacy control. The spec's `untrusted_attributes` list (spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb line 11) also wasn't updated, so the 'doesn't serialize untrusted attributes' test does not cover the new leak.

website_name drops query strings and uses bare rescue on URI parsing

When the domains match, the returned website_name is `host + URI(website).path`, discarding any query string or fragment from the user's URL (e.g. `example.com/page?id=3` becomes `example.com/page`). The PR description says 'show complete URL path', so this silently truncates URLs. Additionally, `URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` swallows all exceptions from malformed URLs; while this returns nil for blanks, a blanket rescue hides unexpected errors — an explicit presence/parse check would be safer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Weak origin check on postMessage handler

The receiver validates messages with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, an unanchored substring test. Any string merely *containing* the discourse origin passes (e.g. an origin like `http://discourse.example.com.attacker.tld` if the forum URL is a substring of it), and the check compares the full URL string against only the origin scheme+host. Use `e.origin === new URL(discourseUrl).origin` for an exact comparison. Impact is limited (message only sets iframe height), but it should be an exact check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: indexOf-based substring validation of postMessage origins is insufficient and should use exact origin matching. The candidate's bypass example reverses the substring direction relative to the quoted code, but it still flags the same validation flaw.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Stored XSS: embed URL interpolated unescaped into raw HTML post TopicEmbed.import builds the post body with `contents << "...#{url}..."` without any HTML escaping, and the resulting post is stored with cook_method raw_html (Post#cook returns raw verbatim, bypassing the markdown/sanitization pipeline). The `url` here is the user-supplied `embed_url` request parameter (only checked with a /^https?:\/\// regex), so a URL containing a single quote and a `, is injected into the post body and rendered unsanitized. The embed view renders it with `raw post.cooked`, so any visitor of the embedded page is exposed to stored XSS. The URL must be escaped (CGI.escapeHTML / ERB::Util.html_escape) and ideally validated with URI.parse.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import caused by unescaped URL interpolation into generated HTML. It does not mention the additional nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the golden comment's XSS issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed crashes when a feed item has no content element

`i.content.scrub` assumes every RSS/Atom item has a `content` element. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements, so any feed item that only provides `description` (or an Atom feed without content) raises NoMethodError on nil. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the whole hourly poll is aborted at the first such item and no further items are imported. Guard with `i.content || i.description` and handle nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that calling `i.content.scrub` crashes when a feed item lacks content, and recommend falling back to `description` with nil handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

The layout embeds `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The controller only validates that the referer's *host* equals embeddable_host; the path/query of the referring URL is attacker-influenced (any page on the embeddable host, or a crafted referer with quotes). A referer containing a single quote or `</script>` breaks out of the JS string literal, allowing script injection into the embed iframe's DOM. Use `escape_javascript`/json encoding for the value instead of raw ERB interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unescaped request.referer interpolation into JavaScript as an XSS vulnerability that can allow arbitrary script execution. The candidate adds specific injection examples and mitigation but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
create_table with force: true will silently drop an existing table

The migration uses `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`, which issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating. If this migration runs against a database that already has topic_embeds data (e.g. it was created outside migrations, or a partial deploy happened), all rows are silently destroyed. The same problem is introduced in this PR by changing db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb to `force: true`, which can drop production top_topics data on environments where the table already exists. `force: true` should only ever be used in development/test schemas, never in shipped migrations.

Import crashes if the existing embed's post has been deleted

In the update branch, `post = embed.post` may be nil (topic/post deleted by moderators, which is common for spam), and the next line calls `PostRevisor.new(post)` on nil, raising NoMethodError. PollFeed runs hourly and TopicRetriever calls it inline, so a single deleted post for a feed URL permanently breaks feed polling for all items after it (retry disabled). Handle a nil post by recreating the topic or skipping.

No error handling around feed fetch; network error kills scheduled job with retry disabled

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` can raise OpenURI::HTTPError, SocketError, timeouts, or RSS parse errors. With `sidekiq_options retry: false`, any transient network failure silently aborts the poll until the next hour with no logging. Wrap the fetch/parse in begin/rescue with logging so transient errors don't go unnoticed.

Anonymous requests can trigger unauthenticated enqueues of retrieval jobs

Any request passing the referer check (which only checks the host header of the referer, trivially spoofable via server-side fetch or a page on the host) with arbitrary embed_url values enqueues a RetrieveTopic job per unique URL. Although TopicRetriever throttles per-URL to once per 60s, an attacker can rotate unlimited distinct embed_url values (all on the embeddable host), each spawning a job that performs an outbound HTTP fetch (or a full PollFeed run) — a job-queue and outbound-traffic amplification vector with no global rate limit.

import_remote does not restrict scheme, enabling file:// reads

TopicEmbed.import checks `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`, but import_remote calls `open(url)` *before* that check, and Ruby's open-uri follows `file://` (and other schemes via redirects). The embed_url comes from the public controller via the RetrieveTopic job. Although TopicRetriever.invalid_host? compares hosts first, a URL like `file:///etc/passwd` has host nil != embeddable_host and is rejected there; however any code path calling import_remote directly (e.g. the disqus thor task with feed data) passes the URL straight to open(). Use an explicit http(s) check before open(), not just inside import.

feed_key is defined but never used, so polling has no modified/etag check

The job defines `feed_key` (apparently intended for caching feed modified state) but never reads or writes it, and poll_feed re-imports every item on every hourly run, re-fetching and re-parsing each item's page via TopicEmbed.import (dedup is by embed_url, so content changes are re-imported even when the feed hasn't changed). Either wire the key into the polling logic or remove it; as-is it is dead code and the comment-implied caching behavior does not exist.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate downsize definition breaks existing 4-argument callers

The class now defines `downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently overrides the first, so the width/height variant is dead code and any existing caller invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height)` now hits the new signature where `dimensions` receives the width integer and `opts` receives the height integer. The dimensions string passed to convert becomes just the width (e.g. "800" instead of "800x600"), producing a malformed ImageMagick resize argument, and opts is a Fixnum so `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise NoMethodError. All existing thumbnail-generation callers of the old API break at runtime.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions, with the second overriding the original width/height signature and breaking callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client limit ignores site settings

The client-side upload validation previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` so it matched the server's per-type configured limits. It now hardcodes 10MB for both images and attachments. On sites configured with smaller limits the client will let a file through that the server then rejects, and on sites with larger attachment limits (e.g. max_attachment_size_kb > 10MB) valid uploads are blocked client-side with a wrong error message. This is a functional regression of the configurable limits.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10MB client upload limit replacing per-type Discourse site settings, causing client-side validation to diverge from configured server limits.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message hardcodes 10MB regardless of server config

The 413 handler now reports "10 MB" as the max size instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When a site has a different max image size configured, the user is shown an incorrect limit in the error dialog, misleading them about what they can upload.

API URL download limit raised to hardcoded 10MB bypassing site setting

The remote-download size cap for API-provided URLs was `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and is now a hardcoded 10.megabytes. This applies to all downloads via the API path (including attachments, not just images that will be downsized), so a site that deliberately lowered max_image_size_kb to limit bandwidth/storage exposure now allows API clients to pull up to 10MB per request from arbitrary URLs, defeating the configured limit.

Downsize loop can silently fail and oversized image still submitted

The loop downsizes to "80%" up to 5 times (max ~33% area reduction) and ignores the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If conversion fails (e.g. ImageMagick error, unsupported format such as SVG or a corrupted image), the loop runs all 5 attempts on an unmodified file and then `Upload.create_for` is called anyway with the still-oversized tempfile. Also, five 20% steps are frequently insufficient for a genuinely large image (e.g. a 40MB photo with a 1MB limit), so the upload will fail with a generic error after the CPU cost of up to 5 image conversions. The downsize result should be checked and a stronger reduction strategy (e.g. scaling toward the target size directly) used.

In-place convert on the same path can corrupt or fail on the source tempfile

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert from[0] ... to` with from == to. ImageMagick reads the input fully before writing, so this usually works, but for animated GIFs the animated path uses gifsicle reading and writing the same file, and any partial write failure leaves the tempfile in a corrupted/truncated state that is then passed to Upload.create_for, potentially producing a broken stored upload. Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original would be safe.

Downsized file keeps original extension/content_type even when format changes

After downsizing, the file is registered via `Upload.create_for(..., filename, ...)` with the original filename and content_type. If ImageMagick's convert writes a different format than the extension suggests (or the animated path produces a different output), the stored upload's extension, content type, and actual bytes can disagree, which can later break thumbnail generation and cause browsers to mis-handle the file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes with nil TopicUser when the user has no topic_user record

TopicsController#unsubscribe does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and then immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. For any logged-in user who never viewed/posted/tracked the topic (e.g. they were watching via a category default or received the email via a group mention), no topic_users row exists, so `tu` is nil and the action raises NoMethodError, returning a 500 instead of unsubscribing the user. It should use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` which creates the record when missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and calling a method on it crashes. The candidate specifically identifies tu.notification_level in unsubscribe.

false_positives.candidate:
State-changing GET endpoint can be triggered by email scanners/link prefetchers

The unsubscribe link in emails is a plain GET to /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe that immediately mutates the user's notification level (topics_controller.rb line 98-116, route added in config/routes.rb line 440-441). Mail clients and security scanners (antivirus proxies, Gmail link scanning, Apple Mail prefetch) routinely GET links in emails without the user clicking them. Any such scan silently mutes the user's topic, or worse toggles them to regular, without consent. Standard practice (and what the existing /email/unsubscribe/:key flow does) is a token-authenticated link or a confirmation page; this endpoint requires only a logged-in session and a guessable numeric topic id, and it also lets any logged-in user flip their own state via CSRF-free GET from any page (img tag on any site they visit while logged in, since there is no CSRF check on GET).

Direct save of TopicUser skips notifications_changed_at, reason, and MessageBus updates

The unsubscribe action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of going through `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is the canonical path: it sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (so the UI shows why the level changed) and publishes a `notification_level_change` MessageBus message to /topic/:id so open tabs update. Saving directly leaves the reason stale (e.g. still 'auto_watch') and other clients' UIs out of sync. Also, an unsubscribe click when the level is 'regular' or below sets it to 'muted', but when it is 'tracking'/'watching' it only drops to 'regular' — a 'regular' user still receives replied-to/mentioned notifications for that topic, so the email's promise 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here' (config/locales/server.en.yml) is not kept for those users.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url} for all callers of MessageBuilder

The shared `unsubscribe_link` locale string now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` (lib/email/message_builder.rb line 90) and `#html_part` (line 67) render this string with `template_args` for any caller that passes `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`; any other caller (plugins, themes, or future core mailers) that enables `add_unsubscribe_link` without supplying `unsubscribe_url` will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and the email will fail to build. A safer design keeps the per-topic sentence in a separate translation or makes the segment conditional.

topicUnsubscribe client route is shadowed by the topic resource's fromParamsNear route

The new route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` is registered after `this.resource('topic', { path: '/t/:slug/:id' }, ...)` whose child route `fromParamsNear` has path '/:nearPost' (a wildcard segment). Because the topic resource is declared first, a URL like /t/my-slug/123/unsubscribe can be matched by topic.fromParamsNear with nearPost='unsubscribe', loading the full topic instead of the unsubscribe page. The unsubscribe route needs to be registered before the topic resource (or the nearPost segment constrained to digits) so it takes precedence.

No tests for the new unsubscribe controller action or route

The PR adds a new mutating endpoint (TopicsController#unsubscribe), new routes, a mailer change, and a locale change, but the only test modification is passing `unsubscribe_url` to an existing MessageBuilder spec. There are no request specs covering: successful unsubscribe, the nil-TopicUser case, the slug redirect branch, or the toggle logic (watching → regular, regular → muted). Given the nil-crash and the mute-vs-regular semantics questions above, these behaviors need test coverage before merging.

`sed -i '' -E ...` uses the BSD/macOS form of in-place editing; on GNU/Linux (Linux CI/dev containers) `sed -i ''` fails with "can't read : No such file or directory". Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak` + remove the backup) or detect the platform.

Cache status timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale, ignoring user locale

The component formats `cacheUpdatedAt` with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the user's selected locale even though the component already has `useLocale()`. All non-English users will see US-formatted dates. Should use the locale from `useLocale()`.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status

On successful cache deletion, the component only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback (which is only passed as `onChanged` in some usages). It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, unlike the disconnect mutation. If `onChanged` is undefined or does not refetch, the UI continues to show the old "Cache Status / Last updated" entry and the "Delete cached data" option even though the cache is gone, until a manual page refresh.

For in-memory delegation credentials (negative credentialId), `CalendarCache` rows are keyed by `userId` + key rather than the (nonexistent) DB credentialId (see `CalendarCacheRepository.getCachedAvailability`). `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` only groups by `credentialId`, so delegated Google Calendar users will never see their cache status and cannot clear it from the UI, even though a cache exists and is actively served. Either look up by userId for delegation credentials or document the limitation.

The groupBy query does not filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. A credential whose only cache rows have expired will still return an `updatedAt` value, so the UI will show a "Cache Status / Last updated" timestamp and a "Delete cached data" action for cache data that is no longer served. This is misleading and lets users trigger a no-op delete with a confirmation dialog.

dev:cron uses npx tsx but tsx is not a declared dependency

The script was changed from `ts-node` to `npx tsx`, but `tsx` is not in dependencies or devDependencies (only `ts-node` is, and it remains unused for this script). `npx` will download `tsx` ad hoc on each run (or fail offline / behind a proxy). Add `tsx` to devDependencies.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares UTC slot hours to organizer-local working hours and computes wrong end

The new working-hours validation computes `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — start and end are identical, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends past workingHour.endTime is never rejected (end should be start + eventLength). Any booking attendee can add arbitrary guests via the API

The handler authorizes any logged-in user whose email matches one of the booking's attendees (`isAttendee`). The UI only exposes this action to the organizer, but the tRPC mutation is callable by any authenticated attendee, letting an external guest with a cal.com account add unlimited arbitrary email addresses to someone else's booking (spam vector, data exposure of the event/ICS to arbitrary addresses). There is also no rate limit and no cap on the number of guests per request. Authorization should be restricted to the organizer / team admin.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` build the EventManager from the calling user. The organizer's credentials (already included in the booking query via `user.credentials`) should be used.

The `add_members` entry is added unconditionally to `editBookingActions`, which is included in `bookedActions` for past and even cancelled bookings (cancel filter only removes the cancel action). Adding guests to a cancelled or already-ended booking still fires calendar updates and sends 'new guests added' confirmation emails for an event that no longer happens. The action should be gated on `!isCancelled` and the booking being in the future.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)

In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup code list is read from the DB, matched, set to null, and written back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code can be replayed and used twice (or more). The update should be conditional/atomic (e.g., compare-and-set in a transaction, or store per-code hash and delete with a WHERE clause that asserts the code still exists).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same backup code before its consumption is persisted, allowing a supposedly one-time code to be accepted multiple times.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code is consumed before the login flow completes

The verified backup code is deleted and the DB updated inside authorize(), before next-auth issues the session/JWT and before the signIn callback runs. If anything downstream fails (signIn callback error, network failure on the client, next-auth internal error), the user's backup code is permanently burned without a successful login, reducing their remaining recovery codes through no fault of their own. Ideally consumption should happen only once login is certain to succeed.

Backup codes unusable for third-party identity provider (SAML/Google) 2FA users

The check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` runs before the backup code branch. Users whose accounts use SAML/Google identity but have 2FA enabled (the totp-link login path) can never authenticate with a backup code: submitting a backupCode without a totpCode always throws, and the login page's 'Lost access' backup-code UI is not offered on the totpEmail path either. These users have no recovery option if they lose their authenticator, despite the feature claiming to provide one.

No test for the core feature: logging in with a backup code

The PR adds backup-code login and backup-code-based 2FA disable, but the only new test coverage clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (and even that doesn't verify file or clipboard content). There is no test that a user can actually log in with a backup code, that a used code is rejected on reuse, that an incorrect code shows the right error, or that disabling 2FA with a backup code works — all explicitly deferred as TODOs. The primary security-relevant code path ships untested.

Both totpCode and backupCode can be submitted; backup code silently takes precedence

When switching between the TOTP and 'Lost access' backup-code views, only one field is cleared in some transitions, and onSubmit spreads all form values into signIn(). The authorize() handler checks backupCode first, so a user who has a stale backupCode value in the form while trying to log in with a TOTP code will get an 'incorrect backup code' error (or worse, succeed via a leftover backup code) even though they typed a valid TOTP. The submit should send only the code relevant to the currently active mode.

Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled

The setup endpoint writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row on every call, even if the user never completes the enable step. A user who starts setup, sees/saves codes, then restarts setup later and completes only the second attempt will have the first set of saved codes silently invalidated (overwritten). Also, codes exist on the DB for users who never enabled 2FA. Generating/persisting codes only on successful enable (or returning them from enable) would make the displayed codes authoritative.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

Crash when destinationCalendar is null: mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration on undefined

In EventManager.create(), `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields undefined when destinationCalendar is null/undefined, and the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining (`evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`). In a collective event with multiple hosts, when EventManager iterates the second host's destination calendar (different credentialId), the event is created on the second host's calendar but the organizer email still points at the first host's calendar externalId. The multi-host fix therefore does not work for CalDAV integrations; the filter should check whether any destinationCalendar entry matches the calendar, or the service should receive the specific destination being targeted.

When creating the booking record, the prisma connect uses `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` only. Any code path that reconstructs the CalendarEvent from the booking without consulting references (e.g. requestReschedule, cancel fallbacks, reminders, payment webhooks) will therefore only see one destination calendar. The per-credential booking references partially compensate, but the persisted booking.destinationCalendar no longer reflects the event's full set of destination calendars.

The rewritten loadUsers no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` for dynamic (non-eventType) bookings, so downstream code that relied on user.organization.slug for dynamic group bookings will now get undefined. Additionally, the new try/catch converts ordinary errors into a generic 500 "Unable to load users" and wraps Prisma known-request errors as 400s, changing the API error contract for dynamic bookings. These changes are incidental to the PR's purpose and untested.

The e2e snapshot updates show `destinationCalendar` in webhook payloads changing from `null` (or a single object) to `[]`/array of objects. This is an outward-facing breaking change to the BOOKING_* webhook payload contract that external integrations depend on; existing consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` or check `=== null` will break. The PR is labeled "non-breaking bug fix" but this is a public API contract change with no migration note or versioning.

In the allRemainingBookings branch inside the per-reference loop, deletion of updated bookings iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(type.endsWith("_calendar"))` rather than the reference's credentialId, and uses only the first calendar reference per updated booking (`updBooking.references.find(...)`). For collective events with multiple calendar references per booking (which this PR introduces), only the first reference's event is deleted per booking, leaving orphaned events on other hosts' calendars; and events may be deleted via the wrong credential, producing 404s.

In createAllCalendarEvents' else branch (no destinationCalendar), the fallback filters `this.calendarCredentials.filter((cred) => cred.type === "calendar")`. No credential in the system has type exactly "calendar" (types are google_calendar, office365_calendar, etc.), so this fallback finds nothing and no calendar event is created at all. No tests added for the multi-destinationCalendar collective booking behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The core change (destinationCalendar becoming an array, per-credential event creation for collective events, multi-reference update/cancel paths in EventManager and handleCancelBooking) is a substantial behavioral change affecting booking creation, reschedule, cancel, and payment webhooks, with several risky code paths (null destinationCalendar, fallback branches). At minimum, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents/updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations and a null destinationCalendar case are needed before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. All dynamic imports are started eagerly at module evaluation; failed chunk loads produce unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")` (and all others) at module-evaluation time, so merely importing `@calcom/app-store` kicks off loading every app chunk immediately — the lazy-loading benefit only applies to bundling, not to runtime loading, and on the server every app module is still loaded whenever app-store is imported. Additionally, if any of these top-level import promises rejects (e.g. a broken app build), it becomes an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the Node process even for code paths that never use that app. Wrap the entries in functions/thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) or attach a rejection handler so failures are surfaced only to the code that awaits them.
