true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Metric tag key inconsistency: 'shards' vs 'shard'

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. The tag name typo means the wait_produce timer cannot be grouped/joined with the other flusher metrics by shard, and produces a second tag key in the metrics namespace for the same dimension.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. The wait_produce metric uses the tag 'shards', while the produce and segment_size_bytes metrics use 'shard', which prevents aggregating these metrics by shard.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarting a 'hung' process can run two flushers on the same shards, producing duplicate segments

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), `process.kill()` is called and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards`. `kill()` is asynchronous — the old process can still be inside its flush loop while the new process starts flushing the same shards. Both processes can call `buffer.flush_segments()` and produce the same segments to Kafka before either calls `done_flush_segments`, resulting in duplicate segments in the buffered-segments topic (duplicate span data downstream). The old process is also never joined, so it is never confirmed dead before the replacement starts. The replacement should only be started after the old process has actually exited (join with timeout), and ideally after verifying no in-flight flush.

Thread-based flusher (produce_to_pipe path) is never killed on restart, so restarts stack threads

When `produce_to_pipe` is set, the flusher 'process' is a `threading.Thread`. On an unhealthy restart, the kill is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, so the old thread is left running and a new one is spawned for the same shards. A hung thread never recovers, so every restart adds another thread; if the hang is caused by a stuck `produce` (as in the backpressure test, where append sleeps), multiple threads will flush the same shards concurrently, duplicating messages. This mostly affects the test path today, but the code claims Thread support, so it should either kill/stop the old thread cooperatively (e.g. per-process stop flag) or refuse to restart thread-based flushers.

Restart counter never resets, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer even if each process is healthy

`process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented; there is no reset after a process proves itself healthy. With MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10, a shard-group that legitimately restarts 11 times over the entire lifetime of a long-running consumer (e.g. due to transient Redis/Kafka failures hours apart) will trigger `RuntimeError` and crash the whole consumer, taking down all shard flushers. The counter should reset (or decay) after a period of healthy operation, as was the case before this change for the single process — but this PR now makes it much more likely since a single misbehaving shard-group among many takes the consumer down.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (the restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` with a process index directly). It also has a bug if it were used: it would overwrite `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous process. It should be removed.

No test that multiple flusher processes actually flush their shards end-to-end

The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts process/shard bookkeeping (counts and map sizes); it never submits a span or asserts that a segment is produced. There is no test covering the core new behavior: that with multiple flusher processes, spans on shards assigned to different processes are all flushed exactly once, nor a test for the restart path (`_ensure_processes_alive` with multiple processes), which is where the trickiest new logic lives. A regression in shard-to-process mapping or in restart handling would pass the current test suite.

submit() iterates self.buffers while restarts mutate it

`submit()` and `_ensure_processes_alive()` run on the main thread, so the dict mutation itself is not racy in-process. However `_create_process_for_shards` replaces `self.buffers[process_index]` with a brand new `SpansBuffer(shards)` each restart. If a restart happens between the `record_stored_segments()` loop and the memory-info loop within a single `submit()` call, some shards' buffers get recorded twice and some not at all within that call; more importantly each restart allocates a new SpansBuffer (with new Redis clients) while old ones are never closed, leaking Redis connections over repeated restarts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

If the same list object is reused across calls (common when a request handler builds fields once and retries, or caches them), the precise-timestamp column is appended repeatedly and leaks into responses/other query paths, potentially causing duplicate columns or unexpected `field` validation errors. The function should copy the list (`selected_columns = [*selected_columns, precise_timestamp]`) before appending.

No such endpoint, URL registration, or handler appears anywhere in this pull request, so for any organization with the `user-feedback-ai-summaries` feature flag enabled, the feedback list page will fire a request that 404s on every load. Either the backend endpoint needs to be part of this change or the hook/component must not ship enabled.

The fields should be derived (e.g. from the exception entry) via the event model rather than read directly from the node dict.

DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200. In a deployment that (accidentally or intentionally) has more than one of these providers on the classpath, e.g. a FIPS environment where keycloak-crypto-fips1402 and keycloak-crypto-default are both present, the non-FIPS provider may win arbitrarily, silently disabling FIPS mode. Either the FIPS provider should have a strictly higher order, or ties among full-featured providers should still be reported as an error.

Most CryptoProvider operations throw UnsupportedOperationException, breaking authz-client features beyond ECDSA signature conversion

The provider registered via META-INF/services in the authz-client jar throws UnsupportedOperationException for getPemUtils(), getCertificateUtils(), getX509CertFactory(), getKeyFactory(), getSignature(), getAlgorithmProvider() etc. CryptoIntegration.init is now called from AuthzClient.create, so if this is the only provider discoverable via the AuthzClient classloader, any code path in keycloak-common/authz-client that touches those APIs will fail at runtime — for example parsing PEM keys/certificates for client JWT assertion signing, or JWKS handling. Previously, these paths worked whenever BC was on the classpath via DefaultCryptoProvider; now a working deployment can regress to UnsupportedOperationException. Each unsupported method should either be implemented with JCE defaults (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or the design should ensure DefaultCryptoProvider is used when available.

Test uses one default-curve key pair for all algorithms and only checks round-trip, not interop with the BC implementation

The test generates a single key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") without specifying a curve, so ES384/ES512 cases run with (typically) a P-256 key and only exercise zero-padding logic, never real 48/66-byte coordinates. More importantly, it only verifies that this provider's conversion round-trips with itself; it does not compare output against DefaultCryptoProvider/BouncyCastle (e.g., BCECDSACryptoProvider) to guarantee signature compatibility with what the Keycloak server produces/expects. A cross-check against the BC implementation per curve would catch subtle encoding mismatches (leading-zero handling, negative integers) that a self-round-trip cannot.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds and lost index writes

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for its whole duration, which (despite the perf cost) guaranteed only one index per NamespacedResource was ever built and published to the cache. Now the lock is only taken around `b.cache[key] = idx`. Two callers can build the same key concurrently: during `searchSupport.init` (multi-worker errgroup) and via `getOrCreateIndex` triggered by a watch event or a Search request arriving while init is still building. Consequences: (1) two bleveIndex objects exist for the same key; the loser of the last cache write keeps getting writes (e.g. from handleEvent) into an index that is no longer in the cache, so those documents silently vanish from search results — data loss for the index; (2) for file-backed indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both builds call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, which will fail (index already exists) or corrupt the on-disk index. getOrCreateIndex's own TODO comment ("we don't want to block while anything is building, just the same key") confirms per-key serialization is required; this change removed even the coarse serialization without adding a per-key one.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race. Narrowing the cacheMu lock to just the cache assignment lets multiple goroutines build the same index for one key concurrently. The candidate adds more detail about consequences, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
NewResourceServer now performs full index build synchronously, changing the constructor contract for all callers

Init() (which builds the entire search index over all namespaces and can take a long time on large installations) is now invoked inside NewResourceServer, and any init failure makes the constructor return an error. Previously, callers such as embedded/in-process usage of the resource server (e.g. apiserver storage wiring, tests, single-binary Grafana where the unified storage may be created alongside other services) got a server immediately and initialization happened lazily or in the background. Those callers now block startup for the whole index build and will fail hard if the index build errors (e.g. transient DB issue during startup), where previously reads/writes could still be served. The PR description itself flags this ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") — the callers of NewResourceServer outside the storage-server target need to be audited; no such audit or feature flag is included.

Failed Init in constructor leaks the server's background context and goroutines

When s.Init(ctx) fails inside NewResourceServer, the function returns nil, err, but s.cancel() is never called. Init may have already started background work before failing — notably searchSupport.init's watch-event goroutine (started after WatchWriteEvents succeeds) and the lifecycle hooks' partial initialization. With no reference to the server retained by the caller, those goroutines and the cancelable context are leaked for the life of the process. The error path should call s.cancel() (or s.Stop) before returning.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in init's worker goroutines

In searchSupport.init, the loop over stats spawns goroutines (limited by initWorkers, so several run concurrently) that both execute `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assign `_, _, err = s.build(...)` where `err` is the outer function-scope variable declared at `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`. These are unsynchronized concurrent read/writes of shared variables — a data race under Go's memory model (and `go test -race` will flag it), and the shared `err` can be clobbered by a later goroutine, causing a real build error to be lost so init reports success with a missing index. Each goroutine should use its own local counter/err (e.g. `i, e := 0, error(nil)` captured per closure), with totals aggregated after group.Wait().

Watch event goroutine has no termination path and panics on closed channel

The goroutine started at the end of init reads `v := <-events` in an infinite loop with no select on a done channel. When the storage backend closes the events channel (e.g. the SQL poller exits when b.done fires on Stop, which closes the stream), the receive yields nil forever and s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) dereferences evt.Type/evt.Key, panicking the process. Additionally, because this uses context.Background(), there is no way to stop it on shutdown. Now that init runs in the constructor for the storage-server target, every server start creates this goroutine, so it must be tied to the server's cancelable context.

Init ordering change: watch events consumed by searchSupport.init but broadcaster started after — event gap risk and misordering rationale

The diff moves initWatcher() to after s.search.init(). searchSupport.init internally starts its own WatchWriteEvents subscription, so this ordering is intentional (watch events are captured while the index builds). However, the server's broadcaster (used by the Watch RPC) is only started after the potentially long index build completes. During that window, Watch RPCs that do reach the server (the gRPC server may already be serving since the module server registers services before/around construction) will fail or block on s.broadcaster — notably s.broadcaster is nil until initWatcher succeeds, so a Watch call during init will nil-pointer panic on `s.broadcaster.Subscribe`. At minimum the nil broadcaster needs a guard, or initWatcher should run before search init (with search's own event subscription providing continuity, which is the pre-existing design).

Storage-server integration test disabled for postgres with no follow-up issue

The only integration test covering the storage-server target (which is exactly the code path changed by this PR — eager init of unified storage at startup) is now skipped for postgres with a TODO comment ("not working with postgres in Drone"). This means the main behavioral change in this PR (synchronous index init at startup) has no integration coverage on one of the two supported databases, and the failure cause is neither diagnosed nor tracked. Since this test is the regression guard for the change, the skip should be replaced by a fix or linked to a tracked issue.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets the shutdown flag on every worker, shuts down every queue.Queue, and joins the threads. Arroyo closes the current strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on partition rebalance/reassignment (e.g. when partitions are revoked and later reassigned, or when running multiple strategies per process). After the first close(), all worker threads have exited, but the factory keeps the same (now dead) pool and creates a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy on top of it. All subsequently submitted items pile up in the dead queues with nothing consuming them: no processing, no offset commits, unbounded memory growth, and the consumer stalls. close() should only stop the strategy's commit thread and drain, leaving pool lifecycle to the factory.

Uses queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown which only exist on Python 3.13+

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown (lines 132, 142). Queue.shutdown and the queue.ShutDown exception were only added to the stdlib in Python 3.13. On any older supported interpreter, importing is fine but calling shutdown() raises AttributeError (caught and logged at line 239-240, leaving workers blocked forever on q.get()) and the except clause referencing queue.ShutDown raises AttributeError inside run, killing the worker thread. Verify the project's minimum Python version or use a sentinel-based shutdown.

Docstring claims backpressure but queues are unbounded

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' (and FixedQueuePool has no maxsize), but each queue.Queue is created with no maxsize (line 185), and submit() never blocks. The arroyo consumer can therefore poll and enqueue messages far faster than workers process them, with the only limit being process memory. Under a slow-consumer backlog this leads to unbounded memory growth and, since processing lags arbitrarily behind, offsets are held back indefinitely while messages accumulate. Either give queues a maxsize so submit blocks, or remove the backpressure claim and add a depth-based guard/metric alert.

Background commit thread commits without regard to partition ownership

The commit loop runs every second and calls commit_function(committable) for all partitions ever seen by the OffsetTracker, including partitions that may have been revoked during a rebalance. Committing offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns violates Kafka consumer-group protocol (the commit is rejected or, worse, races with the new owner). There is no cancellation of in-flight work or clearing of tracker state on partition revocation, and commit also proceeds concurrently with close()/terminate(): shutdown_event is set, but the loop can already be past the wait(1.0) and issue a commit while the pool is shutting down. The strategy needs to stop committing for revoked partitions (e.g. filter against currently assigned partitions passed to create_with_partitions) and re-check shutdown_event before committing.

--max-workers help text/semantics conflate worker threads and queue count

In thread-queue-parallel mode, max_workers sets num_queues (the number of queues, each with one worker thread), and the default when max_workers is None is 20 — whereas in batched-parallel mode the default is ThreadPoolExecutor's default. The shared click option's help ('The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode') hides that for this mode the value also caps per-key parallelism at exactly one thread per queue and that a deploy changing max_workers remaps every group to a different queue (hash(group_key) % num_queues), which can momentarily reorder processing relative to items still in old queues. Consider documenting the remapping caveat and the differing default.

The segment will then be flushed after the shorter root timeout with no root span present, producing a segment whose `is_segment` marker is never set for any span — downstream consumers that rely on exactly one segment span per segment will see malformed output. false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache reintroduces the 'cannot access newly created resource' bug the PR fixes

The permDenialCache entry for (namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder) is set with a 30s TTL whenever a Check is denied, and any later Check with the same key short-circuits to denied before the permission cache or DB is consulted (service.go:116-121). Consider the exact scenario the PR describes: a user without a scoped permission triggers a Check for e.g. dashboards:read on name 'newdash' in folder 'fold1' (e.g. a pre-flight check, a duplicate-name check, or a failed attempt), which populates a denial entry. The user then creates the dashboard/folder, which writes the permission row to the DB. The next Check for that same (user, action, name, folder) hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false without ever re-querying the DB — so the creator is still locked out of their newly created resource for up to 30 seconds. Any mechanism that invalidates/refreshes permCache (e.g. a DB requery triggered by a different resource name) does not invalidate the denial entry, so the denial can even outlive a freshly queried permission map that would allow the request. The denial cache needs to be invalidated when permissions change (e.g. on permission/role writes or resource creation), or its scope/TTL must be bounded so it cannot mask fresh grants.

Denial cache key uses the raw subject identifier, not the resolved user UID

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID (the raw ID parsed from the subject string), whereas the permission cache key (userPermCacheKey) is built from the resolved userIdentifiers.UID obtained via GetUserIdentifiers (service.go:360, 379). Since GetUserIdentifiers accepts both numeric user IDs and UIDs as the subject identifier (service.go:463-469), the same user can be addressed as 'user:112' or 'user:<uid>'. The denial decision was computed from the resolved identity's permissions, but it is stored under the caller-supplied identifier. Consequences: (1) denial entries are not shared between the two spellings, causing unnecessary duplicate DB requeries; (2) if the mapping between a numeric ID and UID ever changes (user deletion/recreation), a stale denial entry keyed by the numeric ID remains valid and keeps denying the new identity for up to 30s. The key should use the resolved UID, consistent with the permission cache.

Denial-cache hits are counted as permission-cache hits in metrics

When the denial cache short-circuits a Check, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit). This conflates the new denial cache with the permission cache, making the permissionCacheUsage metric misleading for operators tuning cache behavior: a denial hit is reported as a permission cache hit even though the permission cache was never consulted. A separate label or metric (e.g. permissionDenialCacheUsage) should be used.

No test covers the denial cache being populated by a denied Check and its interaction with later allowed checks

The only denial-cache test ('Should deny on explicit cache deny entry') manually pre-populates permDenialCache; there is no test that a Check returning Allowed=false actually writes a denial entry and that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits without touching the store. More importantly, there is no test for the interaction the feature exists for: after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant of the permission in the store (simulating resource creation) — the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sibling case where permCache/DB allow but the denial entry denies. Without such a test the stale-denial regression risk (denial entry masking a fresh DB allow) is unguarded.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are canceled when the request context ends

In Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). As soon as the API request returns, the request context is canceled, so the deferred legacy write/delete is aborted with 'context canceled' rather than running for its timeout. This defeats the stated purpose of the mode ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or background) as the parent.

Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy metrics

When d.Storage.Create fails (line 45) or d.Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the legacy store was never contacted. These failures and their durations are attributed to legacy storage, skewing the dual-writer observability data. Both should be recordStorageDuration.

Legacy write failures are swallowed with no logging or reconciliation

Previously, errors from the legacy store were at least logged. In the new goroutines, the error from d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is only converted into a boolean for a metric; it is never logged and no reconciliation/retry is queued. Since mode 3 is the last dual-write stage before cutting over to unified storage, silent legacy failures mean data loss in the legacy store with no operator-visible signal beyond an aggregate counter and no way to recover the missed write.

Legacy Update reuses the request's objInfo, so legacy can write different data than storage

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so the legacy store received exactly the object that unified storage wrote (via updateWrapper). The new code passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update in a goroutine, so the legacy store re-computes the updated object from its own (possibly stale) current state. If legacy and unified have diverged (e.g., an earlier async legacy write was canceled or failed), the legacy copy can end up with different content than the authoritative unified copy. The updateWrapper mechanism was removed without a replacement guarantee.

Legacy Delete failures on NotFound are treated as errors

The old Delete tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy store (expected when an object exists only in unified storage, which is the common case in mode 3 after migration backfill gaps). The new code records any legacy Delete error, including NotFound, as a failure metric. In mode 3, objects created before backfill will routinely 404 in legacy, producing persistent false failure signals.

Unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens

Mode 3's defining behavior is 'write to unified, then asynchronously write to legacy', but none of the tests assert that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are invoked (e.g., via m.AssertExpectations or waiting on the goroutine with mock.AssertEventually). The tests return immediately after the unified call, so the goroutines may not have run; a regression that drops the legacy write entirely (or is canceled immediately, as in the context bug) would still pass. Also the error-path test cases set up legacy mock expectations that are never exercised or verified.

TestMode3_Get creates its own registry instead of the shared one

TestMode3_Get declares a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while every other mode-3 test uses the package-level `p`. This is inconsistent and, if the dual writer registers metrics in NewDualWriter, would panic on double registration in other tests or mask registration issues; the unrelated change to TestMode1_Get that moved `p` to package scope suggests this local declaration is an oversight.

Interpolating before the $__range guard defeats the no-split check for range-variable queries

runSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on each target before the partition step. The subsequent querySupportsSplitting() check relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) detecting a literal $__range/$__range_s variables in the expression (see the comment at querySplitting.ts:285-287: queries with $__range must not be split because the backend interpolates $__range against the split sub-range). After applyTemplateVariables runs, $__range has already been replaced with the full original time range, so isQueryWithRangeVariable never matches and such queries are now split into per-day chunks with the full-range value baked into the expr. Every sub-request then aggregates over the whole range instead of its chunk, producing duplicated/incorrect data for any query using $__range. The interpolation must happen after the range-variable check, or the check must run on the pre-interpolation expression.

Double template interpolation in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery now interpolates every target via datasource.applyTemplateVariables(), but the resulting queries are then passed to runSplitQuery(), which (after this PR) calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on the same targets (querySplitting.ts:299). Template interpolation is not idempotent in general: if a variable's value itself contains text that looks like a variable reference or a `$` character (common in label-filter values, regex patterns, or chained variables), the second pass will re-interpolate the already-substituted value and corrupt the expression or step. Either runShardSplitQuery should skip interpolation and let runSplitQuery do it once, or runSplitQuery needs a way to know the targets are already interpolated. There is also no test covering this double-interpolation scenario.

$__auto and other interval macros are frozen to the full-range value across all split chunks

By interpolating with datasource.applyTemplateVariables before splitting, built-in macros like $__auto (and any interval-derived variable) are resolved once against the original request's range/interval and then reused verbatim in every sub-request's narrower time range. Previously the backend resolved these per sub-request, allowing each chunk to use a range-appropriate value. The new test in querySplitting.test.ts ('Interpolates queries before execution') hard-codes the expectation that $__auto becomes 5m for all three daily chunks, which codifies the behavior change; for range-sensitive macros this can change results (e.g., count_over_time windows no longer adapting per chunk). This should be confirmed as intended and, if so, documented, since it silently changes query semantics for existing dashboards.

Count-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded

CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices in one session and, if the count is below deviceLimit, performs the insert in a separate session/transaction. Two (or many) concurrent requests from different new devices can each observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-insert must be atomic (e.g. a single conditional insert/transaction with a lock, or a unique count constraint) to actually enforce the limit under load, which is exactly the scenario (burst of anonymous requests) this feature targets.

There is no mapping of this sentinel error to an appropriate HTTP status (e.g. 403/429) or user-facing message anywhere in this PR, making the feature effectively brick anonymous access without explanation once the limit is hit (combined with the cache bug, intermittently).

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

The store then neither updates nor deletes the stale row, so the device stays locked out until the 61-day cleanup job removes it.

If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device ID is still marked as tagged in the 29-minute local cache. On the user's next request, the cache hit makes tagDeviceUI return nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. false_positives.candidate:
AnonymousDeviceLimit exposed to all frontend clients including anonymous users

AnonymousDeviceLimit is included in the frontend settings DTO served to every requester, including unauthenticated/anonymous visitors. This leaks an instance's configured capacity limit (useful reconnaissance for abuse: an attacker knows exactly how many spoofed X-Grafana-Device-Id values are needed to lock out legitimate anonymous users, since the limit is enforced per arbitrary client-supplied device IDs). Consider only exposing it to signed-in admins, or not exposing it at all if no frontend code consumes it — no frontend usage is added in this PR, only the type declarations.

New device_limit setting is undocumented and lacks validation

The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting is parsed with MustInt64(0) but has no documentation (configure docs/conf defaults), and negative values are not rejected. A negative value behaves like 0 (limit disabled) due to the `deviceLimit > 0` check, silently ignoring the user's intent; a validation error for negative values would be clearer. Also note that device_limit interacts with the 61-day retention (keepFor) in impl.go while the limit counts only devices active in the last 30 days — this asymmetry is nowhere documented for operators.

Fallback locales are never loaded outside of the ApplicationController#set_locale path

I18n.translate loads only `config.locale` (line 68) before delegating to the real translate, which will now walk the fallback chain defined by FallbackLocaleList (user locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en). The fallback locales are only pre-loaded via ApplicationController#set_locale's `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call. Any translation performed outside a web request — background jobs (Sidekiq), mailers, rake tasks, one-off scripts — will look up keys in fallback locales that were never loaded, so the Fallbacks backend will return 'translation missing' strings instead of the English/default text. The accelerator should ensure all fallback locales for the current locale are loaded inside `translate`/`load_locale`, not rely on the controller filter.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, serving stale translations after default_locale changes

The cache key is built from `key`, `config.locale` and the backend object id. With this PR the effective translation for a given I18n.locale also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (via FallbackLocaleList#[]). When an admin changes default_locale at runtime, the fallback order changes but the cache key does not, so previously cached results from the old fallback chain keep being served for up to LRU_CACHE_SIZE (300) entries until they age out. There is no I18n.reload!/cache invalidation hooked to the default_locale SiteSetting in this change, so users in a non-default locale will continue seeing translations from the old default locale. The key should incorporate the fallback locales (or the cache should be cleared when default_locale changes).

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but only overrides [], so all other Hash behaviors report it as empty

FallbackLocaleList is a Hash whose lookup semantics are entirely in `[]`, with no stored entries. Any code in the i18n gem, Rails, or plugins that interacts with `I18n.fallbacks` through Hash methods other than `[]` (e.g. `each`, `key?`, `keys`, `merge!`, `store`) will see an empty hash: per-locale fallback rules configured that way are silently dropped, and any code that iterates the fallbacks map (for preloading, validation, or locale resolution) will do nothing. Subclassing Hash while making `[]` lie about the contents is fragile; a plain object responding to `[]` (and to whatever the i18n version in use requires) would be safer, or the entries should actually be stored in the hash.

Fallback lookup dereferences SiteSetting.default_locale on every translation, which is not safe during boot or before SiteSetting is available

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` calls `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` on every translation lookup. During application boot (initializers, eager loading, asset precompilation) or in contexts where the settings table/connection is not available, SiteSetting may raise or return nil; `nil.to_sym` yields a symbol that then goes through the load path and could trigger DB queries or errors at times when translations are used before the app is fully initialized. A safer approach is to memoize the fallback list and only refresh it when the setting actually changes, and to guard against SiteSetting being unavailable.

Initializer relies on implicit filename ordering ('order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb') which is fragile

The comment at the top states the file must load after 02-freedom_patches.rb, and this happens to work because Rails loads initializers alphabetically and digits sort before letters. But the i18n initializer's `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` must apply to the backend class before it is used, and the pluralization include replaces the removed config/initializers/pluralization.rb — whose old filename sorted before i18n.rb, so any load-order dependent behavior (e.g. plugins or freedom patches touching I18n) silently depends on string sort order. If anyone renames this file (e.g. to `20-i18n.rb` or adds a locale-related initializer), the ordering requirement breaks with no error. The dependency should be explicit (require the freedom patch file, or use config.initializer with `before`/`after`), not a comment.

The migration uses `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`, which issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating. If this migration runs against a database that already has topic_embeds data (e.g. it was created outside migrations, or a partial deploy happened), all rows are silently destroyed. `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` can raise OpenURI::HTTPError, SocketError, timeouts, or RSS parse errors. With `sidekiq_options retry: false`, any transient network failure silently aborts the poll until the next hour with no logging. Wrap the fetch/parse in begin/rescue with logging so transient errors don't go unnoticed.

Any request passing the referer check (which only checks the host header of the referer, trivially spoofable via server-side fetch or a page on the host) with arbitrary embed_url values enqueues a RetrieveTopic job per unique URL. Although TopicRetriever throttles per-URL to once per 60s, an attacker can rotate unlimited distinct embed_url values (all on the embeddable host), each spawning a job that performs an outbound HTTP fetch (or a full PollFeed run) — a job-queue and outbound-traffic amplification vector with no global rate limit.

The embed_url comes from the public controller via the RetrieveTopic job. Although TopicRetriever.invalid_host? compares hosts first, a URL like `file:///etc/passwd` has host nil != embeddable_host and is rejected there; however any code path calling import_remote directly (e.g. the disqus thor task with feed data) passes the URL straight to open(). feed_key is defined but never used, so polling has no modified/etag check

Either wire the key into the polling logic or remove it; as-is it is dead code and the comment-implied caching behavior does not exist.

postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The client-side upload validation previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` so it matched the server's per-type configured limits. On sites configured with smaller limits the client will let a file through that the server then rejects, and on sites with larger attachment limits (e.g. max_attachment_size_kb > 10MB) valid uploads are blocked client-side with a wrong error message. The remote-download size cap for API-provided URLs was `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and is now a hardcoded 10.megabytes. This applies to all downloads via the API path (including attachments, not just images that will be downsized), so a site that deliberately lowered max_image_size_kb to limit bandwidth/storage exposure now allows API clients to pull up to 10MB per request from arbitrary URLs, defeating the configured limit.

The loop downsizes to "80%" up to 5 times (max ~33% area reduction) and ignores the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If conversion fails (e.g. ImageMagick error, unsupported format such as SVG or a corrupted image), the loop runs all 5 attempts on an unmodified file and then `Upload.create_for` is called anyway with the still-oversized tempfile. Also, five 20% steps are frequently insufficient for a genuinely large image (e.g. a 40MB photo with a 1MB limit), so the upload will fail with a generic error after the CPU cost of up to 5 image conversions. The downsize result should be checked and a stronger reduction strategy (e.g. scaling toward the target size directly) used.

Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original would be safe.

After downsizing, the file is registered via `Upload.create_for(..., filename, ...)` with the original filename and content_type. false_positives.candidate:
State-changing GET endpoint can be triggered by email scanners/link prefetchers

The unsubscribe link in emails is a plain GET to /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe that immediately mutates the user's notification level (topics_controller.rb line 98-116, route added in config/routes.rb line 440-441). Mail clients and security scanners (antivirus proxies, Gmail link scanning, Apple Mail prefetch) routinely GET links in emails without the user clicking them. Any such scan silently mutes the user's topic, or worse toggles them to regular, without consent. Standard practice (and what the existing /email/unsubscribe/:key flow does) is a token-authenticated link or a confirmation page; this endpoint requires only a logged-in session and a guessable numeric topic id, and it also lets any logged-in user flip their own state via CSRF-free GET from any page (img tag on any site they visit while logged in, since there is no CSRF check on GET).

The unsubscribe action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of going through `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is the canonical path: it sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (so the UI shows why the level changed) and publishes a `notification_level_change` MessageBus message to /topic/:id so open tabs update. Saving directly leaves the reason stale (e.g. still 'auto_watch') and other clients' UIs out of sync. Also, an unsubscribe click when the level is 'regular' or below sets it to 'muted', but when it is 'tracking'/'watching' it only drops to 'regular' — a 'regular' user still receives replied-to/mentioned notifications for that topic, so the email's promise 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here' (config/locales/server.en.yml) is not kept for those users.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url} for all callers of MessageBuilder

The shared `unsubscribe_link` locale string now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` (lib/email/message_builder.rb line 90) and `#html_part` (line 67) render this string with `template_args` for any caller that passes `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`; any other caller (plugins, themes, or future core mailers) that enables `add_unsubscribe_link` without supplying `unsubscribe_url` will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and the email will fail to build. A safer design keeps the per-topic sentence in a separate translation or makes the segment conditional.

The new route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` is registered after `this.resource('topic', { path: '/t/:slug/:id' }, ...)` whose child route `fromParamsNear` has path '/:nearPost' (a wildcard segment). Because the topic resource is declared first, a URL like /t/my-slug/123/unsubscribe can be matched by topic.fromParamsNear with nearPost='unsubscribe', loading the full topic instead of the unsubscribe page. The unsubscribe route needs to be registered before the topic resource (or the nearPost segment constrained to digits) so it takes precedence.

The PR adds a new mutating endpoint (TopicsController#unsubscribe), new routes, a mailer change, and a locale change, but the only test modification is passing `unsubscribe_url` to an existing MessageBuilder spec. There are no request specs covering: successful unsubscribe, the nil-TopicUser case, the slug redirect branch, or the toggle logic (watching → regular, regular → muted). Given the nil-crash and the mute-vs-regular semantics questions above, these behaviors need test coverage before merging.

Prisma's sql tag does NOT bind a JS array as a single Postgres array parameter — it expands array elements into separate positional placeholders (which is why Prisma.join exists for IN lists). Unless BookingTimeStatusDenormalized is a live view or is populated by a trigger/denormalization job that runs synchronously on booking insert, the table will not contain the new row and the assertion will fail (or pass vacuously if rows are absent). The PR author notes the tests were never executed due to runner configuration issues, so this is unverified.

That request fails, the thrown error is caught by the surrounding try/catch which aborts the whole loop, and all remaining email reminders in the batch are left uncancelled (and their DB rows undeleted) for that run. The per-reminder SendGrid cancel request is inside a single try/catch wrapping the whole loop. false_positives.candidate:
Crash when destinationCalendar is null: mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration on undefined

In EventManager.create(), `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields undefined when destinationCalendar is null/undefined, and the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining (`evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`). The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was null-safe. Any booking where destinationCalendar is null and location is Google Meet (e.g. handleNewBooking now explicitly sets destinationCalendar to null when neither eventType nor organizer has one) will throw a TypeError and abort booking creation.

Organizer email forced to first host's destination calendar externalId even when event is created under a different host's credential

In createEvent (and updateEvent), the organizer attendee's email is overridden with `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId` — always the FIRST entry of destinationCalendar — regardless of which credential/selectedCalendar the event is actually created on. In a collective event with multiple hosts, when EventManager iterates the second host's destination calendar (different credentialId), the event is created on the second host's calendar but the organizer email still points at the first host's calendar externalId. This produces events attributed to the wrong organizer, can break Google Meet conference creation tied to the organizer, and causes mismatched organizer identity across hosts' calendars.

createEvent silently falls back to "primary" when destinationCalendar has no entry for this credential

`calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"` means that when destinationCalendar is non-empty but none of its entries has a matching credentialId (e.g. credential not in the list, or a stale destinationCalendar pointing at a removed credential), the event is silently created on the current credential's primary calendar instead of the intended destination. Combined with the 404-is-swallowed behavior in CalendarManager.createEvent, this can create duplicate/misplaced events on the wrong calendar with no error surfaced. It should log/skip when an explicit destination was requested but not found for this credential.

CalDAV createEvent only honors the first destinationCalendar, so collective multi-host events are not created on other hosts' calendars

BaseCalendarService.createEvent destructures only `[mainHostDestinationCalendar]` and filters calendars by that single externalId. Since EventManager now iterates all destinationCalendar entries and calls createEvent once per credential, a second host using a CalDAV-based calendar (Apple/iCloud/etc.) will have their event filtered out because their destination's externalId is never compared — only the first host's externalId is. The multi-host fix therefore does not work for CalDAV integrations; the filter should check whether any destinationCalendar entry matches the calendar, or the service should receive the specific destination being targeted.

Only the first destinationCalendar is persisted on the booking row, losing other hosts' calendars for later operations

When creating the booking record, the prisma connect uses `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` only. For collective events where evt.destinationCalendar contains multiple hosts' destination calendars, only the organizer's is connected to the Booking. Any code path that reconstructs the CalendarEvent from the booking without consulting references (e.g. requestReschedule, cancel fallbacks, reminders, payment webhooks) will therefore only see one destination calendar. The per-credential booking references partially compensate, but the persisted booking.destinationCalendar no longer reflects the event's full set of destination calendars.

loadUsers rewrite changes error behavior and drops organization selection for dynamic bookings

The rewritten loadUsers no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` for dynamic (non-eventType) bookings, so downstream code that relied on user.organization.slug for dynamic group bookings will now get undefined. Additionally, the new try/catch converts ordinary errors into a generic 500 "Unable to load users" and wraps Prisma known-request errors as 400s, changing the API error contract for dynamic bookings. These changes are incidental to the PR's purpose and untested.

destinationCalendar payload shape changed from null/object to array — breaking change for webhook consumers

The e2e snapshot updates show `destinationCalendar` in webhook payloads changing from `null` (or a single object) to `[]`/array of objects. This is an outward-facing breaking change to the BOOKING_* webhook payload contract that external integrations depend on; existing consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` or check `=== null` will break. The PR is labeled "non-breaking bug fix" but this is a public API contract change with no migration note or versioning.

Recurring all-remaining cancellation deletes with the wrong credentials when references carry credentialIds

In the allRemainingBookings branch inside the per-reference loop, deletion of updated bookings iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(type.endsWith("_calendar"))` rather than the reference's credentialId, and uses only the first calendar reference per updated booking (`updBooking.references.find(...)`). For collective events with multiple calendar references per booking (which this PR introduces), only the first reference's event is deleted per booking, leaving orphaned events on other hosts' calendars; and events may be deleted via the wrong credential, producing 404s.

Fallback branch filters credentials by type === "calendar" but credential types are integration-specific (e.g. google_calendar)

In createAllCalendarEvents' else branch (no destinationCalendar), the fallback filters `this.calendarCredentials.filter((cred) => cred.type === "calendar")`. No credential in the system has type exactly "calendar" (types are google_calendar, office365_calendar, etc.), so this fallback finds nothing and no calendar event is created at all. It should filter by type.endsWith("_calendar") (excluding other_calendar) or pick the first calendar credential, as the old code effectively did via destinationCalendar.

No tests added for the multi-destinationCalendar collective booking behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The core change (destinationCalendar becoming an array, per-credential event creation for collective events, multi-reference update/cancel paths in EventManager and handleCancelBooking) is a substantial behavioral change affecting booking creation, reschedule, cancel, and payment webhooks, with several risky code paths (null destinationCalendar, fallback branches). At minimum, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents/updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations and a null destinationCalendar case are needed before merging.

false_positives.candidate:
All dynamic imports are started eagerly at module evaluation; failed chunk loads produce unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")` (and all others) at module-evaluation time, so merely importing `@calcom/app-store` kicks off loading every app chunk immediately — the lazy-loading benefit only applies to bundling, not to runtime loading, and on the server every app module is still loaded whenever app-store is imported. Additionally, if any of these top-level import promises rejects (e.g. a broken app build), it becomes an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the Node process even for code paths that never use that app. Wrap the entries in functions/thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) or attach a rejection handler so failures are surfaced only to the code that awaits them.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not a promise — deletion failures are silently ignored on paid-booking cancellation

In the paid-booking branch, `await apiDeletes;` awaits a plain Array (which resolves immediately), so none of the calendar/video deletion promises pushed into apiDeletes are actually awaited before returning "Booking successfully cancelled.". Combined with this PR's change to push into apiDeletes from an async forEach callback (line 460-470), deletions may not even have been started yet. Use `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)` so integration deletions complete (and failures are observed) before responding.
